articles.title: Democratic Socialist Principles in the Book of Acts
articles.author: DSA Religion and Socialism Working Group
articles.content: The Mediterranean sun beat down upon the dusty limestone streets of Jerusalem, casting sharp shadows across a city fractured by imperial occupation, grinding poverty , and rigid social stratification. On the surface, the Roman peace—the Pax Romana —reigned supreme. But beneath that veneer lay a harsh economic reality: wealth was concentrated in the hands of a tiny elite, temple elites exacted heavy tributes, and the margins of society were choked with day laborers, widows, and orphans always on the brink of starvation. Yet, among a clandestine gathering of believers who had recently embraced the resurrected Galilean teacher, a radically different world was being born. Luke, recording these events in the Book of Acts, captures a moment in human history where the fundamental rules of survival were rewritten. Standing in the courtyard, watching these Jesus followers unburden themselves of their deeds, scrolls, and surplus wealth, one could hear the quiet hum of a new social order taking shape. This was not merely a spiritual revival; it was an embryonic blueprint for a democratic socialist society. The Abolition of Destitution: Reclaiming the Commons To walk among the early Jerusalem believers was to witness something entirely alien to the ancient world: the total eradication of destitution. Luke writes in Acts 4:34–35: There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. When property owners liquidated their estates, they were enacting structural redistribution. As Luke notes, “no one claimed that any of their possessions was their own, but everything was held in common” (Acts 4:32). In modern political economy, this mirrors the core tenets of democratic socialism : the belief that the material prerequisites of life—housing, food, security—are human rights, and that surplus capital must answer to human need rather than private hoarding. The Jerusalem church instituted a micro-economy where wealth was stripped of its power to oppress, ensuring that basic human dignity was guaranteed for every member of the community . Participatory Democracy and the Feminist Critique: Solving the Crisis of Equity Eventually, every radical movement faces an administrative crucible, and the early church was no exception. As the community grew, cracks began to show. In Acts 6:1–7, a serious crisis of equity erupted: the Hellenistic (Greek-speaking) Jewish widows were being systematically overlooked in the daily distribution of food in favor of the Hebrew widows. In any other ancient institution, this administrative failure would have been handled from the top down by an autocratic ruler issuing decrees. But the apostles’ response anticipated the core mechanisms of participatory democracy . They did not hide behind closed doors to draft a corporate fix. Instead, as Acts 6:2 records, “the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples.” They brought the systemic failure directly to the people, acknowledging that administrative power belonged to the community. They established a transparent, democratic process: Decentralization of Power: Authority was shared rather than hoarded at the top. Community Vetting: The broader assembly was tasked with selecting leaders from among themselves—traditionally recorded as men of good repute, full of the Spirit and wisdom—to manage the communal treasury and welfare distribution. Accountability: The newly appointed administrators were directly accountable to the public they served. However, a critical historical and feminist lens—championed by contemporary theologians and scholars such as Meggan Watterson —forces us to look closer at who was actually doing the heavy lifting of survival and community care. Watterson’s work on alternative and marginalized early Christian texts (such as Mary Magdalene Revealed and The Girl Who Baptized Herself ) underscores how patriarchal structures often whitewashed or edited out the active, frontline leadership of women . While the canonical text of Acts tells us that male deacons were appointed to solve the Greek-speaking widows’ crisis, feminist biblical scholarship suggests that women were the vital connective tissue of these early house-church economies. They were the ones hospitality-girding, networking, and sustaining communal life on the ground. The actual survival of the community depended heavily on women’s unrecognized or under-reported labor . The distribution to widows was not merely a top-down handout managed by men, but a grassroots crisis solved because marginalized voices—the neglected Hellenistic widows—refused to be rendered invisible and demanded systemic equity. Voluntary Association vs. Coercion: The Philosophical Bridge Critics often point out a fundamental tension when comparing the Jerusalem church to modern democratic socialism: the early believers operated through voluntary spiritual devotion, whereas modern socialism often utilizes state legislation, public policy, and taxation to achieve equity. There was no Roman legion, no temple police, and no state decree forcing citizens to liquidate their assets. The redistribution in Acts was entirely voluntary. Yet, despite the difference in enforcement mechanisms, both systems seek to move human society away from a predatory, survival-of-the-fittest ethos toward a cooperative commonwealth. While democratic socialists use the lever of the democratic state to shield citizens from the predations of unregulated capital, the early church used the power of communal solidarity to achieve that same goal: a society where no one is left behind to suffer the indignity of poverty. The Messy Reality of Commune Life: Ideals vs. Unfinished Chores It is easy to romanticize the Book of Acts as a utopian snapshot of a society where everyone lived in frictionless harmony. But anyone who has ever been in an intentional community or a cooperative knows that political alignment does not automatically erase human friction. Any commune member can readily testify to the corrosive power of unwashed dishes, passive-aggressive chore wheels, and ego clashes to erode solidarity—even when every member is on the same political and ideological page. A broader reading of the Christian Bible shows that the early church was plagued by these same dysfunctions. The letters of Paul to the Corinthians, Galatians, and Romans reveal communities riven by squabbles, socioeconomic elitism (even during the communal Love Feasts or Lord’s Suppers), petty power struggles, and failed attempts at radical solidarity. The Jerusalem church itself eventually suffered severe economic collapse, requiring Paul to spend years organizing a massive international collection across the Gentile churches to bail out the impoverished Jerusalem believers. The radical sharing depicted in Acts was a messy, high-stakes experiment in human cooperation. The fact that it often fractured under the weight of human selfishness and administrative strain does not invalidate its democratic socialist principles. Rather, it humanizes them. It shows that economic justice is not an automatic spiritual state but a daily, difficult practice of negotiation, accountability, and grace. From Capitalism to Community The narrative preserved in the Book of Acts remains a powerful historical and moral provocation. Long before Karl Marx penned his critiques of industrial capitalism or modern democratic socialists campaigned for universal healthcare and housing, a small band of believers in Jerusalem proved that human beings could organize their economic lives around equity, shared labor, and radical care—even if the housekeeping, the gender exclusions, and the internal squabbles made it infinitely more complicated than the highlight reel suggests. Whether viewed through the lens of divine intervention or sociopolitical history, the early church blueprint challenges every modern economy to answer a timeless, haunting question: Why should anyone suffer in need when there is more than enough to go around? For further reading: Bauckham, Richard. Jesus and the Eyewitnesses: The Gospels as Eyewitness Testimony . Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing Co., 2006. Hengel, Martin. Property and Riches in the Early Church: Aspects of an Early Christian Social History . Fortress Press, 1974. Kootstra, Paul. “Christian Socialism and the Early Church: Reading Acts in Modern Political Contexts.” Journal of Theological Politics , vol. 42, no. 3, 2018, pp. 145–162. Stassen, Glen H., and David P. Gushee. Kingdom Ethics: Following Jesus in Contemporary Context . InterVarsity Press, 2003. The Bible . English Standard Version (ESV). Crossway Bibles, 2001. (Specifically referencing Acts 2:42–47, Acts 4:32–35, Acts 5:1–11, and Acts 6:1–7). Watterson, Meggan. Mary Magdalene Revealed: The First Apostle, Her Feminist Gospel & the Christianity We Haven’t Tried Yet . Hay House, 2019. Watterson, Meggan. The Girl Who Baptized Herself . Hay House, 2024. articles.title: Fall is Here but Prices Aren’t Falling: Protestors Rally Against Iran War, for Divestment as Gas Prices Skyrocket
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: By: Liam Noble BOSTON COMMON – On Saturday, October 3, anti-war protesters and left organizations rallied against the multiple simultaneous illegal wars prosecuted by the United States under the current regime — with a particular focus on the war in Iran. Protestors and local activists including Rabbi Greg Hersh and Tony Van Der Meer gave speeches condemning the loss of life caused by imperialist violence, especially in Latin America and West Asia. The atmosphere at the protest was one of shared outrage: against the illegal wars of aggression, the insanity of the US leadership, as well as over the deaths of and intentional targeting of civilians. At least two signs carried photographs of dead children, their gravesites, or of family photos from when they were still alive. The message spoke for itself even as many vocalized: “We Want The Murder to End Now.” The life lost was staggering and never far from the center stage of protest. The number of dead children is particularly chilling: 247+ in Lebanon, 350+ dead children in Iran, tens of thousands of dead in Palestine. More than 220 fishermen in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean have been murdered by the US military in senseless drone strikes. The blockade of Cuba has also been tightened, with the U.S. intercepting $3 million in fuel shipments the week of the rally alone, working people suffering and dying because of the loss of electricity to homes and hospitals. The United States stands also on the brink of potential invasion of Cuba itself. Increasingly, the intentions of the US empire might be seen as waging a war on life. One rallying cry in a speech by prominent Massachusetts Peace Action activist Paul Shannon was a cardinal demand: “the state should get pension funds away from murderous military contractors.” This demand to separate state employee investments, or divestment, shows the depth and pragmatism of the struggle. Rabbi Greg Hersh speaks to the crowd (Liam Noble) Nationalist Counterprotesters The anti-war event became tense when counterprotestors arrived. Persian nationalists, or Pahlavi supporters, carried large flags showing Pahlavi, Trump and Netanyahu shoulder to shoulder, the national flags photoshopped to blend into one another. If nothing else, the display was a true expression of the Pahlavi movement— farce to encourage the waging of the conflict and intimidate the peace activists. A man with a bullhorn, wearing a Persian nationalist flag as a cape, screamed “USA, USA,” in an attempt to drown out the speakers. When a woman approached him to ask the aggressor to stop, he put the bullhorn in her face and screamed, “Terrorist, terrorist.” A short time later, he tried to enter the crowd and disrupt the event, but some mischievous comrade broke his bullhorn in half, leaving him despondently carrying a broken piece of it in each hand. At no point could the counterprotestors muster more than two people for their cause. Pahlavi counter-protestor with broken megaphone (Liam Noble) War Felt at the Gas Pump The most prominent aspect of the peace protest was opposition to the war on Iran. The most visible and tangible conflict, the Iran war is a new energy conflict. It is one of many of the wars, the pain of which is felt at the gas pump itself. Diesel, the life-blood of commercial transportation, averages $6.50 in Massachusetts – roughly double what it was at the beginning of the year. While higher gas prices can trigger a decrease in car usage by regular consumers who rely on personal vehicles, diesel is far less elastic : widely used in construction, railways, and trucking, the supply chains themselves are heavily and institutionally reliant on diesel. Additional shortages of industrial lubricants and petroleum byproducts will continue to have knock-on effects of price inflation. These effects cannot be underestimated; one expert has called the likely impact inflation “turbocharged” beyond record numbers. All of these factors all but assure the international tightening of petroleum supply is likely at the very least to result in a worldwide recession. In principle, the war itself is a crime, let alone the social murder caused by its externalities, but it’s remarkable to reflect on the incompetence with which it was pursued. The Iran War seems executed on impulse, with no plan. Perhaps initiated under the assumption of a mere three-day war, a weekend war, that the Islamic Republic would capitulate similarly to Venezuela following Maduro’s abduction if the leadership were murdered. Instead, Iran was prepared and immediately struck back on vulnerable American positions. Within a week, Naval Support Facility Bahrain— the logistics headquarters of the US fifth fleet— was destroyed, and will probably never be rebuilt. Subsequently, aircraft carriers like USS Abraham Lincoln were forced to withdraw from the area because keeping them properly supplied proved impossible. The radar sites in the region used to gather early warning and telemetry against Iranian ballistic missiles were also destroyed with drones. This leaves the US/Israeli axis critically vulnerable to the most effective and well-stocked weapon Iran has: ballistic missiles. Should the war heat up again (which seems positively inevitable), it is bewildering how vulnerable Israel’s position appears. Buttressed only by ideological fanaticism, the position of the Israeli state itself could become totally unsustainable under concentrated missile fire on its cities, infrastructure, and sensitive military sites. This has not yet come to pass because of the calculations around the potential use of nuclear weapons, and an Iranian desire to show restraint in escalation. Tony Van Der Meer speaking to the crowd (Liam Noble) At the rally, a frequent question asked was: “How do you think this will end?” The better question is probably, how will this all end up ? Its corollary answer: In an unfamiliar world. But probably not anytime soon. The curious position of war protest this year is that the Iran War is very different from the Vietnam War, or the Iraq War, or even the contemporary blockade against Cuba. Iran is a middle-tier power, a nation fighting a war of national defense. This is not an American war against a poorly-organized adversary, or against a near-defenseless civilian population; rather, the conflict is peer/peer between states. In the context of this war, the United States is a weakened country, no longer hegemonic, throwing the last of its strength at an entrenched and prepared enemy with significant moral investment and landed base. The result is that the United States has been decisively defeated and pushed out of the region. All this is to say, regardless of flareups of the future, the United States lost a war, and lost it badly and quickly. The illusions of American fighting power seemed to have vanished quicker than a glass of neat whiskey left around Secretary Hegseth. What then is the responsibility of anti-war protestors? To champion the cause of peace, of course. And to use their activism to restrain the American military, to prevent other possible wars, to illuminate the foul intentions and terrible crimes; and to delegitimize the wars wherever they are pursued. Liam Noble is a Boston DSA member living in Somerville and a contributing writer to Working Mass. articles.title: Who’s Your Uber Driver on the Phone to? Welcome to the Long, Long Diaspora Call
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: The back of an Uber (Working Mass) By: Nesrine Malik This article was originally published by The Guardian on September 30, 2026. The question of the week is: “who are Uber drivers always talking to on the phone?” It’s one that regularly surfaces on Reddit threads and social media and even, on a couple of occasions, in the office. It’s not my question (I know who they are talking to), but I think the fact that many people are so baffled by it tells us a lot about the separate worlds we occupy. When you get a cab on a ride-hailing app, the chances that your driver will be on the phone is high. The conversation is almost always quiet, containing pauses so long that it often seems they are actually no longer on a call. But then comes a rejoinder, a laugh, an interjection, and the marathon continues. For anyone of an immigrant background, the question of who they are talking to is absolutely no mystery. They are talking to us; their siblings, parents, cousins and friends. Sometimes the person on the end of the line is back home, other times they are in a western city also navigating the dislocations of immigrant life. The long phone call is a regular feature of diaspora lives, and even more so for those employed in long, solitary work such as cab driving. These conversations are about nothing and everything. This is not an exhaustive list, but based on the calls I constantly field from friends and family, the content I receive in a follow-up call, and familiar themes from chats with drivers in Arabic (which I sometimes get drawn into), the subjects are remarkably consistent. The range includes family gossip, wedding updates, complaints about the cost of living in the west, advice on navigating complex immigration systems, extremely detailed health updates, and political analysis of whatever crisis is unfolding. These conversations can broadly be sorted into one of two categories: “serious technical resolution of a problem” or “shooting the breeze”. In my experience, these beast mode long phone calls are between someone on a long shift, commute or drive, and a mother cooking in the kitchen. There is a languorous quality to the call. Time and conversational convention shift to accommodate long silences without explanation, as one person or the other breaks away to get on with something – dismount or park or blitz something in the food processor. Because the point is not the actual chat. It is a broadly phatic – that is to say language used for bonding – form of communication, an exercise in yearning and homesickness. It helps us bridge a gap between long distances and absences, and simulate a proximity that is so deeply longed for. The interminable phone call is an immigrant’s lifeline, now made cheap and stable by voice over IP (the ability to make calls on an internet connection). But it is also a feature of broader cultural and economic patterns. Western time is personal, individual, literally “me time”, something that is violated if demanded without permission. This time is parcelled out necessarily for decompression, for work, for leisure. In other cultures, time is social and public. In Sudan, for example, there is no such thing as calling ahead before a visit. Your home is a drop-in destination from about 11am onwards. A neighbour will pop in for a chat, a relative will be driving home and swing by, and if there are children in the household, their own social lives mean you just never know how many people you are cooking for. The corner shop is a lifeline of last minute provision as numbers swell unexpectedly. If you are an introvert, good luck. When that physical socialisation is impossible, the phone does the work. Certain conditions make the visit and the call possible. Homes where there is often a homemaker to receive, or work that does not require strict, in-office professional deportment and execution. Highly structured working environments and fast-paced modern lives mean that entire societies are firmly post-casual-phone-call. In these contexts, I find myself so wary of ambushing or alarming people with a call that I send a clear warning beforehand. No, there is nothing to worry about, and are you sure this is a good time to speak? Absolutely no worries if not. Inside of an Uber from passenger (Working Mass) But it is also a mindset, which you can lose over time. I find myself becoming increasingly post-phone call outside work, constantly thinking to myself that I will ring a relative back when I have the time. Generally, I prefer to message or voice note, conscious that when I return the call, it absolutely will not be a quick and efficient catch up. But, in truth, I do have the time, I have just assimilated the same rigid notions of downtime and non-urgent phone calls as an incursion. Fundamentally, this is an extremely capitalist notion of time as purely a function of work, where even if you are not working, you are “re-charging” in anticipation of more work. The fact that the long driver call is such a bewildering anomaly is a meeting of those two worlds. In one, a passenger cannot fathom that you might have so much to say to someone over the phone, because everyone you love or want to see is generally within your immediate social reach, and because it is unfathomable to dedicate so much of your precious bandwidth to seemingly aimless conversation. In another, loved ones are in a different country or sprawl all over the world, and without their constant companionship life is just alienation and monotonous work. But I suspect there is more to the lost art of the phone call in certain societies than just the pressures of modernity. In contemporary life, there are so many ways to feel like you are in touch and in conversation when you are not. So many ways to feel part of some slipstream of humanity, when in fact we are scrolling, meme-ing, seeing news from friends and strangers alike via story updates, while not exchanging anything meaningful or even uttering a single word. Those in exile are acutely aware of alienation, and reach out to remedy it. But for those in their home countries, loneliness still lurks in ways harder to recognise. A phone call is honestly less time consuming and more replenishing than anything else we use our devices for. Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist and the author of We Need New Stories: Challenging the Toxic Myths Behind Our Age of Discontent . The post Who’s Your Uber Driver on the Phone to? Welcome to the Long, Long Diaspora Call appeared first on Working Mass .

articles.title: Tech Workers’ Leverage Over Employers Is Shifting
articles.author: JS Tan
articles.content: Not long ago, tech companies courted their workers. Engineers were scarce enough that anyone who felt mistreated could quit and land somewhere else within weeks, so employers kept them around with generous perks and wide latitude on the job, and many firms took pains to look like the progressive institutions their staff expected them to be. That arrangement fell apart around 2022. Rising interest rates made executives far less willing to spend on their workforce, and many of them came to see their own employees’ activism as a problem to be crushed. Layoffs followed, aimed with notable precision at troublemakers, while the industry’s leaders bent the knee to Trump. JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine spent years trying to unionize this industry, and their new book , Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry , is unusually frank about what has and hasn’t worked. Their main argument is that the standard union campaign, which keeps the drive quiet until a majority signs on and saves open confrontation for the contract fight, fits tech badly. When factory workers walk out, production stops. Tech workers often have no idea where their leverage lies, as the New York Times Tech Guild learned when a well-organized strike on Election Day failed to disrupt operations. Tan and Redwine argue that workers will only find their leverage by picking fights with management over concrete grievances, long before anyone brings up the word “union.” Eric Blanc spoke with them about the chill that has settled over the industry, the promise and pitfalls of unionizing tech, salting, and whether artificial intelligence might push more coders to see themselves as workers. Eric Blanc What is the overall state of tech worker organizing under Trump 2.0? It seems like lots of people must be angry with their companies’ capitulation to Trump, but I imagine the fear factor is also a lot higher today. JS Tan Yes, we’re hearing from fellow organizers and tech workers that there are many people, especially at the larger tech companies, who are upset with their employer cozying up with Trump. This is related to the perhaps more salient change in the industry since about 2022, which is that tech employers have, as a whole, also adopted a far more anti-worker posture. Previously, tech workers had a lot of individual bargaining power because they were in such demand. If a job didn’t treat them well, they could just leave for another one. So to make sure workers stayed, employers showered us with perks, gave us a lot of discretion in our jobs, and, importantly, frequently lived up to the progressive values that many employees expected. But in 2022, two things changed. First, interest rates shot up (a response by the Fed to cool COVID-19-induced inflation), which made employers far less willing to spend lavishly on tech worker salaries or perks. Second, many tech employers shifted to the right and cozied up to Trump because of their own employees’ unrest — which they saw as being fueled by progressive politics, or, as one newly minted trillionaire would put it, the “woke mind virus.” These two things meant that tech companies weren’t just all of a sudden laying off employees to cut costs, but explicitly targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) folks, AI ethics teams, content moderation roles, and the like — all in an effort to reset the balance of power between workers and management. This is, we think, what many workers are upset about — not just that their employers are now capitulating to Trump, but that many have embraced a kind of conservatism in an effort to stave off the progressive politics that existed previously and underpinned worker resistance. Clarissa Redwine What all this means for organizing is that workers are more proletarianized. Compared to the late 2010s when many of our organizing conversations were about trying to convince tech employees that they were in fact workers, this is more or less no longer an issue. Now instead the problem is whether workers are willing to organize in this much more risky environment and in a labor market that no longer favors them. Since about 2022, this chilling of the industry’s labor relations has resulted in far less organizing — reaching perhaps its lowest point in 2024 and early 2025. But now what we’re seeing is new organizing emerge, this time based mostly on issues of AI. Eric Blanc In Against Tech Oligarchy , you argue that the traditional model of unionization didn’t work in tech. Can you explain what the obstacles were and what strategic takeaways you draw from that experience/impasse? JS Tan At its core, we think that the traditional union organizing playbook isn’t designed for the particularities of the tech labor process — and we say this as people who for many years believed in and tried to push this playbook onto the tech industry. The traditional playbook assumes that workers know beforehand where their leverage is; and in most workplaces, certainly in a factory or a school or a hospital, that leverage is very clear, alongside what might threaten or alter this leverage. When factory workers walk off the assembly line, nothing gets built, and profit halts. But tech is quite different. A day’s work can, on one day, be worth nothing and on another generate fabulous profits, all depending on factors outside the immediate control of the worker. This is perhaps most clear in the strike: a powerful, high-participation strike in tech would do little to stop a tech company from continuing to make money. That’s in fact exactly what we saw when the New York Times tech workers went on strike for their contract. They were a super-militant shop, planned their strike [to coincide with] the most important day of the year — the day of the presidential election — and secured high participation in their strike pledge, only growing support day after day on the picket line. Yet when they struck, nothing (major) broke, and the pressure that they had banked on failed. Clarissa Redwine That is why organizing in tech requires a different approach — one that allows and even encourages workers to explore their leverage. And in fact, because tech workers are such a heterogeneous bunch and do such different work on a day-to-day basis, we’d even expect that different teams, different roles, and employees at different companies would all hold different kinds of leverage, and that is something that needs to be interrogated. Eric Blanc Which sectors and campaigns do you think are most strategic for tech worker organizing, around both material and political (anti–Immigration and Customs Enforcement, antiauthoritarianism, anti-Trump, etc.) demands? Are there any employees in particular whose structural power can be more readily leveraged? Clarissa Redwine We’d argue that the movement never really cracked the code on how we organize the most powerful companies in the sector. The cloud hyperscalers, for instance, are a critical choke point in the AI stack and also in the industry as a whole. These are behemoth companies with hundreds of thousands of workers and thus an example of why the traditional union playbook won’t work. The issues you mentioned — anti-ICE organizing, antiauthoritarianism — are issues that we need to take on today, yet it’ll take a decade or more to organize such a large and spread-out company for union recognition. JS Tan The problem with structural power when it comes to tech work, however, is that a large portion of workers sit under the firm’s R&D division. And so this means that they are inherently future-oriented — building a new feature or incubating a new product and the like. Yes, maintaining these products/features is also a big job, but that’s not how these workers spend the majority of their time. This future-orientation means that withholding labor won’t hurt present profits. And so, we need to think strategically about who within each company, within each business model, has immediate power. That’s not something we have a generic answer for — and it’s in fact something that every campaign across every company needs to be thinking about depending on their business model, where they sit in the tech-ecosystem, what their firm’s competitive advantage is, and so on. Eric Blanc One less traditional approach to unionizing in tech is via premajority unionism (“minority unionism”), an approach I’m sympathetic to but that I’ve heard in practice in tech has sometimes resulted in unions being cliquey pockets of self-selecting leftists. What’s your impression on the balance and prospects for premajority unionism in tech? JS Tan Premajority unionism is the reality for many workers in tech, especially those working at larger companies. That’s what the workers at Google have gone with. Any major tech company, with tens or hundreds of thousands of workers, would likely have to go with this approach because winning recognition for such a large unit would take years. Clarissa Redwine From our perspective, we’re actually agnostic about whether a union is National Labor Relations Board recognized (i.e., a majority union) or a minority union, as long as it is a fighting union. And in fact the solidarity, premajority union at Google is a good example of this. They aren’t recognized, but that hasn’t stopped them from fighting and winning their demands with a minority of workers. In fact, acting as a union, where workers aim to win material gains from the boss, is critical at every stage in training militant organizers who can wield collective power at each stage of growth. The goal is not to stop growing and fight for only a minority of workers but rather to fight with the people you have in service of growth, demonstrating the value of collective action to workers who are new to the fight and practicing the mechanics of forcing concessions from management. Eric Blanc One thing I loved about your book is that you were very sober about the strengths and limitations of all efforts to date, and you don’t assume there is a proven model or path yet for how to organize this sector. On the other hand, at the end of the book I was hoping to read a bit more about what your hypotheses are about potential ways forward. My impression is that maybe the sweet spot for the foreseeable future is to organize and mobilize tech workers around widely held and deeply felt issue-based campaigns, without framing these as necessarily steps to unionization from the start. JS Tan At the start of the tech worker movement, demands were concrete. When workers wanted their company to disengage from the military, they took collective action to push for that specific thing. And the experience of taking collective action together, and seeing how the boss responded, was a radicalizing event for many tech workers. When organizers shifted to building toward recognized unions, putting off clashes with the boss to fuel growth, demands became more abstract, complex, and distant. Asking a coworker to stand with you against systemic sexism or brutal on-call policies is a much easier task than asking if they believe in unions. The experience of fighting for material change together is a far more powerful tool for building pro-union sentiment among your coworkers than any one-on-one conversation about what might be possible to win in a contract or about the history of the labor movement. In short, organizing shifted from concrete, familiar demands to more abstract and distant goals, aiming to reach the largest number of supporters possible before taking action. And for many tech workers, this new approach to organizing, what we call in our book “the Recognition Playbook,” ended up delaying the critical experience of taking part in direct class conflict. This not only reduced the number of workers who saw the mask drop when they pressured the boss; it also atrophied organizers’ ability to find and embrace effective leverage. Clarissa Redwine The hurdle right now in tech organizing is that workers haven’t discovered where their leverage is. To find out, we think, workers need to engage in class conflict and find opportunities to experiment with exercising leverage. That is in fact what we think is one of the big issues with the traditional union playbook: that it intentionally delays or avoids class conflict. In your typical campaign, organizers are always trying to bring new workers into the fold of the union drive, but the drive is all along meant to remain secret. And so what organizers do is have these one-on-one conversations with their coworkers until everyone is bought into the union, at which point you vote for the union and become recognized. Sometimes international unions will suggest running a shop-wide issue campaign where the goal is to sign on more union members (not to win material gains), but besides that, workers never actually engage in any direct conflict with the bosses through this whole process. Only in the end, when they go on strike while bargaining their contract, do workers finally get to experience class conflict — but by that point it is too late: workers in tech will never have had the chance to practice exercising their leverage, or get a glimpse of the boss’s counteroffensive. JS Tan Workers need to organize with a conflict-forward mindset. They need to encourage class conflict so that workers can start to figure out how to organize in a way that can actually threaten their employers’ bottom line. Eric Blanc What do you think about the prospect of recruiting young people to salt tech? It seems clear to me that tech is an extremely strategic industry. I’m not sure why we wouldn’t want to orient to getting salts in there, even if primarily to boost issue-based campaigns at first. Clarissa Redwine I actually salted at my first tech job after the Kickstarter union drive, and that was an incredible experience. Tech workers are hungry for autonomy, social good, and security. The challenge is showing coworkers what a fighting union is in practice before ever bringing up the U-word, which can divide workers who would have otherwise been united behind a specific demand. Salting is going to be crucial in tech moving forward and there is an organic movement of tech workers who’ve left or been pushed out of their union drives who go on to salt independently, joining the next company with an intent to unionize. However, salting in a more traditional way where an international targets a specific company is extremely difficult because of the nature of tech work where jobs are highly specialized. JS Tan The tech industry is extremely heterogeneous and that means not all companies are going to have the same kind of importance in the industry as a whole. Organizers should move towards the critical chokepoints or otherwise key campaigns to support them. However, proactive, targeted salting is not always possible. Because of this challenge, many tech workers have adopted the perspective that they will organize wherever they land. And that is a very exciting cultural shift in labor, where workers are salting whether they are backed by an international or all on their own. Eric Blanc Do you think the introduction of AI into tech workers’ workflows and their companies will potentially create openings for larger numbers of workers seeing themselves as expendable and precarious workers in need of organization, like skilled factory workers did a century ago when Taylorist attacks on their autonomy pushed them into unionizing? JS Tan For many workers, yes — agentic coding systems have in many ways made it impossible for workers to really see coding as this artisanal craft, as many did previously. But there is also a group who see themselves as “high-agency” workers and hope to use these agentic coding systems to accelerate their careers. And in fact, these two wolves can exist in one person. For instance, a worker can feel proletarianized by these new AI developments in the field, yet may be motivated to double down on using them because they are worried these tools will narrow the window for future job/career mobility (i.e., the permanent underclass) — and so, they may embrace grind culture and 9–9–6, largely for individualistic reasons. Clarissa Redwine The feeling among many tech workers is that AI is a reserve army that will do your job for zero salary and never sleeps. You can either adapt, or be replaced. But when your company is no longer pretending to be stewards of public good, and they are actively trying to force you down and out, then workers naturally start to question why they should be building this tech in the first place. So although there is increased precarity, workers still hold the keys to their employers’ bid in the AI race, and that is an opportunity that can revitalize the tech worker movement and shift the ground under the tech oligarchy as we know it. articles.title: Mark Carney Isn’t the “Leader of the Free World.” Lula Is.
articles.author: Gerard Di Trolio
articles.content: The headlines say it all: “Meet the New Leader of the Free World. No, It’s Not Donald Trump.” “ Canada’s Carney Claims Mantle of ‘Leader of the Free World.’” “How Mark Carney Became Leader of the Free World by Standing Up to Trump.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is not just incredibly popular at home but, increasingly, around the world. Now there is even talk of him winning the Nobel Peace Prize . It is a comforting fiction for those terrified by Donald Trump. But if any leader deserves such a title, it is not Canada’s ex-banker prime minister but Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The reason is simple: Lula has done more to protect democracy and promote a fair global system than Carney has. And the point is more than academic. Lula will face off with Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president who attempted to overturn Brazil’s last election, on October 25 in the second round of the presidential election. The contest will determine whether Latin America’s biggest democracy maintains its resistance to the global far right or rejoins its ranks. The contrasts between Carney and Lula are clearest in their respective paths to power. While Carney did not come from an elite family, his path in life took him to Harvard, Oxford, and then Goldman Sachs. He led the central banks of two of the world’s largest economies. And as his recent investment summit has shown, he has the global economic elite in his Rolodex. Lula came from an impoverished family and was largely raised by his single mother. He became a trade union leader in the ABC Region of Greater São Paulo, was jailed for his union activism, and lost part of a finger in a workplace accident as a metalworker. Carney has spent his career at home among elites; Lula helped to restore democracy to Brazil after a military dictatorship that lasted more than twenty years. Lula’s Vision of Democracy Any conversation about Lula’s role in defending democracy must begin with Brazil’s response to those who tried to overthrow it. After pro–Jair Bolsonaro mobs stormed government buildings in Brasília on January 8, 2023, mere days after Lula took office, his government treated the attack as a serious threat to the constitutional order. Brazil’s justice system ultimately convicted and jailed Bolsonaro for plotting a coup that also targeted Lula for assassination. But the response was not limited to the courts. In September of that year, Lula issued a presidential decree that created the Observatório da Democracia (Democracy Observatory), which monitors threats to Brazilian democracy. Lula’s conception of democracy is also worth noting: it extends beyond voting and elections. At the launch of the Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty in July 2024, he stated , “Hunger and poverty inhibit the full exercise of citizenship and weaken democracy itself.” On the third anniversary of the January 8 events, Lula gave a speech where he said of democracy: It’s more than the desire and the right to vote on Election Day — and then keep your voter registration card for the next four years. Democracy requires the effective participation of society in government decisions. He also noted that given the levels of inequality in Brazil, strong and effective democracy requires a country “with more rights and fewer privileges.” Lula’s partnership with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez in the “In Defence of Democracy” initiative further demonstrates his effort to make democracy a central part of Brazil’s international role. By linking free elections and constitutional institutions with social inclusion, reduced inequality, pluralism, and resistance to right-wing extremism and disinformation, Lula has helped advance a broader conception of democracy in international affairs. This is what support for democracy looks like in a world where the United States has dropped the pretense of even caring about it. More countries ought to step up on that front, but so far under Carney, Canada has not. Moral Consistency? Lula has been criticized in the past for not doing enough to address the collapse of democracy in Venezuela. However, after the flagrantly stolen 2024 elections, Brazil refused to recognize the results and blocked Venezuela’s bid for BRICS partner status. The Brazilian government has also criticized Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega’s laws that have essentially ended competitive elections in the country. While Nicaragua and Brazil no longer have ambassadors in each other’s capitals, full diplomatic relations have not been ruptured. Nor has that happened with Venezuela. Lula has never shut the door to diplomacy. After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, he condemned the invasion but also offered Brazil as a mediator. Some will criticize this approach as being too conciliatory. But diplomacy as a tool of statecraft has come under great strain since 9/11 and America’s war on terror. Talking to the other side gets smeared as being naive at best and legitimizing evil at worst. Lula has been unusually consistent in championing diplomacy when other leaders have not. Compare this to Carney. When Trump launched the war on Iran, Canadian government officials provided contradictory statements condemning military action without United Nations approval while insisting that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon. Between March 5 and 10, Carney left the door open to Canadian participation in the war before ruling it out after five days when it became clear that it was unpopular. Minister of National Defence David McGuinty’s comment, “The prime minister and the government decided from the beginning of this that we would support this incursion, but we’re also calling for a diplomatic end to it,” sums up the contradiction. In recent days during the opening of the UN General Assembly, when Carney was asked about Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran, he responded with: “Well, there is a war underway, and he’s speaking the language of war.” He also made sure to remind everyone that Iran is one of the biggest threats in the world — and a threat to Israel. Israel provides one of the biggest contrasts between Carney and Lula. Less than three weeks after October 7, Lula called what Israel was doing to Gaza genocide . The Canadian government has yet to take such a position. And it has only done the bare minimum in the face of the genocide. While the government restricted some arms-related exports that could be used in Gaza, it continues to allow exports for use in the Iron Dome . The Carney government’s cavalier attitude toward these modest restrictions was on display when it demoted Sean Casey, the parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs. Casey was removed from his position after voting for a New Democratic Party bill that would have closed shipping loopholes, which currently allow military goods exported to the United States to be sent onward to active conflict zones. While Canada also sanctioned violent West Bank settlers and joined the ban of imports from illegal settlements in the West Bank, it has never shown any actual leadership on the issue — it has merely followed the meager steps of European countries. The government has also quietly defined anti-Zionism to be antisemitism on the Public Safety Canada website. The difference on this issue could not be starker between the two leaders. With Trump’s national security policy declaring that the Western Hemisphere essentially belongs to the United States, Carney has decided to pretend that Canada is part of Europe, abandoning the Americas. Lula on the other hand has been rallying other Latin American and Caribbean countries to reject the Donroe Doctrine. There is also a very telling difference in how Brazil and Canada have responded to Trump’s blockade of Cuba. Brazil has called it “illegal and illegitimate,” while Canada has announced that it is “monitoring the situation.” Canada has reliably voted at the UN for an end to the decades-long US embargo. But when Brazil denounced the blockade at the UN, Canada abstained on the procedural vote to open debate on it. Lula has articulated a grand democratic vision, while Carney seems to be trying to somehow salvage the Western-led global order without the United States. That is a quixotic project: it is impossible to do without Washington, and it totally ignores the shift in global economic power now underway. It’s Still the Economy, Stupid As Lula once again fights for his political life against a Bolsonaro, while also contending with American meddling in the election, it is important to remember how fragile democracy can be and who actually fights for it. But the defense of democratic institutions is not, by itself, sufficient. Democracies also require political orders capable of eliciting the allegiance of their populations. Carney’s famous Davos speech was an exercise in political mythmaking with little substance . It put on offer little more than a revamped technocratic neoliberalism — the very model whose failures helped create the political disillusionment exploited by Trump. The point isn’t that Lula is infallible. The Workers’ Party and Brazilian left have not produced someone credible to succeed him . There is also ample reason to criticize the way legitimate concerns about disinformation on social media have bled into state-backed erosion of free speech — a development that factions of the Left have themselves attacked . Lula’s approach to the economy also deserves scrutiny. Shortly after his return to power in 2023, economist Matías Vernengo argued that his government should abandon overly restrictive fiscal frameworks in order to “expand public investment and promote higher wages and consumer credit.” On the eve of the presidential election, Vernengo acknowledged that Brazil’s economy had indeed grown under Lula and that unemployment was low. But he also noted how the fiscal framework he criticized in 2023 had held growth below what was possible, adding, “People eat GDP. What they don’t eat is democracy.” The first-round results of the Brazilian presidential election offer a warning about the potential political cost of that failure. This gets at one of the main contradictions of Lulismo : the president acknowledges the need for inclusivity and development to protect democracy but can be overly cautious on the economic front. This is the inverse of Carney in many ways. The Canadian prime minister does not pontificate about democracy and, while there is every reason to be skeptical of the kind of growth Carney’s economic policies will promote, has put economic growth at the center of an effort to reorient Canada’s economic relationships. For now, he has largely set aside concerns about the deficit. He remains wildly popular in Canada well over a year after his election. That should be a major signal to the Left. Economic growth matters if the Left is to achieve its goals, create political legitimacy, and protect democracy. Ultimately, whatever Lula’s domestic limitations, the values he espouses on the global stage should guide democracies in these uncertain times, not Carney’s technocratic and status quo sensibilities. Realizing that global vision will require both economic equality and growth at home. articles.title: Could AI Fix Climate Change? Probably Not Under Capitalism.
articles.author: Noah Gordon
articles.content: “There’s no question that in four or five years’ time, we’re going to use a lot more fossil fuel,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told Ezra Klein of The New York Times . “But also, in the next decade in front of us, at no time in history are we better prepared to move to sustainable energy,” he added. “If you want to turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable, lean into AI.” It is perhaps surprising, given the tone of much mainstream discussion of artificial intelligence, that the man at the helm of the world’s most valuable company, which produces chips essential to the new technology, was agnostic about whether AI would stop climate change. “It could be solar, it could be nuclear, it could be fission, fusion, hydro, you name it,” Huang said in his hour-long interview with Klein. The future would be great, but he was uncertain about how. His rhetoric is a prime example of how the language of climate politics, and of climate obstruction, has changed since the emergence of powerful AI models. Save Us How? In a way, Huang’s rather vague promises are a return to the rhetoric of the early days of climate politics, when economists like Nobel Prize winner William Nordhaus won renown for models that heavily discounted the future compared to today. By this thinking, spending lots of money now to avoid climate damages later was not worth it because future humans would be so rich that they could afford the climate costs. The model was called “ DICE ”; humans should roll one. Why try to predict what exactly human ingenuity would deliver? In 2013, Nordhaus simply assumed a “backstop technology . . . that can replace all fossil fuels.” More recent Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change models explicitly expect carbon removal to do much of the cleanup work, somehow growing a thousandfold in two or three decades even though deploying this public good doesn’t make anyone any money. Sometimes tech oligarchs are more specific. DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis highlights the promise of advancements in material design, wondering if AI might deliver the “perfect battery.” Anthropic chief Dario Amodei pins his hopes on “atmospheric carbon removal and clean energy technology [and] lab-grown meat,” while the investor Reid Hoffman says AI “could help the people building fusion power.” Google Brain cofounder Andrew Ng believes AI could improve the science on the “possibility of cooling Earth via stratospheric aerosol injection,” this solar geoengineering technology being, along with carbon removal, the favored tool of the overshoot ideology that asserts humans can break the climate now and put it back together later. To be fair, it would be unreasonable to expect a full explanation of a technology that has yet to be invented, especially in the waning minutes of a podcast that Huang spent flailing, blithely dismissing fears about models that are already hacking governments and businesses and deceiving the firms that built them. If AI became superintelligent, human intelligence, dwarfed by that of the machine it had created, would struggle to predict what it might achieve. Could a dog fathom the existence of antibiotics, or a deer the purpose of a wildlife crossing? It is not impossible that AI achieves or helps humans make unbelievable technological breakthroughs well before the mid-century climate targets that occupy policymakers’ attention. The technology is already capable of predicting the structure of proteins and outperforming people on humanity’s hardest tests. Economists without conflicts of interest, like a team led by Nicholas Stern at the London School of Economics, underline AI’s potential to improve weather forecasting, make solar and wind power more efficient, and make alternative proteins more competitive. AI boosters like Huang are not necessarily dishonest; rather, their subject is inherently uncertain. Still, it seems that the people busy building world-changing technology have not thought about the links between technology and political economy in a capitalist system, where even well-meaning AI firms may not be able to risk slowing down research for fear that their competitors in Silicon Valley, or in China, won’t. Amodei thinks his product is so strong that “ideology will not survive” it! Plus, fossil fuel firms have access to ChatGPT too: indeed, a recent study in Nature found that AI-driven productivity gains in the gas and oil sector, such as cheaper and more accurate drilling, would outweigh improvements in the renewables sector. Technological progress does change political and business incentives, and the development of a truly impressive energy-storage technology would indeed make it easier to run the world’s grids on renewables. But it wouldn’t necessarily get the owner of a gas power plant or pipeline to shut down their assets before they’re amortized. Some industries, like carmakers, are decarbonizable . Others, like coal mining, are not — for them, the existential risk is not the rising seas but the changing of the guard. Big fossil fuel firms pursue profitable energy investments for their shareholders, which is not always the same thing as pursuing low-cost technologies. Deny, Deny, Deny This word, uncertainty, is essential. It has played a key role in the rhetoric of climate reaction and in the key argument thereof, climate denial. For years, the reactionary tactic was to muddy the waters so that humans may continue to muddy the atmosphere. As long as it seemed even halfway plausible, reactionaries cast doubt on whether humans were changing the climate at all. As the evidence has mounted that anthropogenic climate change is real and dangerous, these claims have fallen out of fashion, with the noteworthy exception of the man at the top of the US government, Donald Trump. “The people that say AI is going to destroy the World, and that Data Centers are bad for your neighborhood, are the same people that said, just a short time ago, that the World would be extinguished by ‘Climate Change,’” Trump posted on Truth Social in September, days before making a similar point at the United Nations. “That HOAX never worked out for them, and now they’re on to the next one.” There are other parallels between the discourses on AI and climate risk. The warnings from inside frontier labs — the lead of Alignment Science at Anthropic cheerfully admitted “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans” — resemble the warnings from the Exxon scientists who discovered in the 1980s that their product might overheat the planet. The oil firm’s executives responded to the sound of the whistle by launching a decades-long disinformation campaign about the risk. Nvidia’s Huang, the man making the marvelous chips and increasingly providing the financial backstop for AI data centers, now wants everyone to calm down: “All the alarmism, all the doomerism, all of the predictions — they’re scaring people.” Playing on uncertainty is not the only option available to climate obstructionists. Most rhetoric by those who oppose climate action is in line with reactionary rhetoric throughout history. In 1991, the year governments formally began negotiating the UN’s climate treaty, the scholar Albert O. Hirschman published a treatise on the subject, titled The Rhetoric of Reaction . Drawing on examples going back to Edmund Burke’s denunciation of the French Revolution, Hirschman identified three types of rhetoric deployed against efforts to change the world: progressive plans could be depicted as “perverse” if they would allegedly aggravate the problem they were meant to solve, “futile” if they would achieve nothing, and as a source of “jeopardy” if their implementation would endanger some other value. A climate example springs to mind for each. Don’t stop burning gas in Louisiana, as it would be perverse: China would simply burn even dirtier coal in response. It would be futile to steer humanity from energy-dense fossil fuels to effete renewables — and our country is only responsible for a tiny share of emissions anyway. To restrict fossil fuels would be to jeopardize economic growth and freedom. Hirschman’s classic schema has held up quite well for the subsequent thirty-five years of climate rhetoric, as evidenced by how well more recent scholarship on climate obstruction comports with it. And What Was the Bad News? What’s so interesting about the AI uncertainty is that it goes in both directions. Superintelligence could help solve the climate crisis — the term deus ex machina feels a bit on the nose, given that Elon Musk speaks of a “digital God ” and Sam Altman speaks of “ magic intelligence in the sky.” Or it could destroy human civilization! If either outcome is likely, there’s not much use subsidizing the production of wind turbines today or worrying about how many people might die of extreme heat in fifty years. In other words, the likelier you believe AI is to achieve superintelligence, the less urgent climate change seems, whether the superintelligence is aligned or malign. Perhaps this helps explain why some on the Left are quick to dismiss the potentially dangerous or salutary effects of AI. Noam Chomsky was an early and prominent skeptic of the idea that models could truly reason. The left-wing writer Cory Doctorow says spreading fears about AI, a business he calls “hooking up statistical engines to money-furnaces,” just helps hyperscalers raise capital. This is why the historian Rutger Bregman even argues that “ AI denial ” is a problem of the Left, just as climate denial has been one of the Right. As Hirschman’s book notes, reactionaries have “no monopoly on simplistic, peremptory, and intransigent rhetoric.” Perhaps the AI companies do want to show their product is powerful in order to attract investment, or to demonstrate that it’s dangerous so the US government will build a moat to protect their gigantic data center investments. But just because their warnings may be self-interested doesn’t mean they’re wrong about the power of the technology. The failure of a few overextended players in the AI economy — Oracle , anybody? — would not prevent the technology from changing the world. Since when is the Left so blasé about what damage giant high-tech businesses might wreak in the pursuit of profit? For the climate-minded left, it may feel as if the wrong crisis has suddenly seized the world’s attention, even as climate impacts keep worsening. (In the week that Anthropic warned of “existential risks to humanity” in its IPO prospectus, Bangkok was underwater .) There is some history here. When environmental concerns were first raised in in the 1960s and ’70s, some dismissed them as distractions from more important issues. But the world is, unfortunately, not limited to one existential risk at a time. Those who have worked to stop nuclear war have seen many other risks come and go since the United States bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Artificial intelligence is clearly a powerful technology: no one should dismiss this because they prefer to mock the tech elites building it. The primary concern at present should be that this technology is emerging into a global economic system dominated by profit seekers, largely unconcerned with the climate crisis, whom governments are for the most part allowing to regulate themselves. While some have compared the current AI build-out to the Manhattan Project, nuclear technology was never allowed to remain in private hands. If AI is to help solve the climate crisis without causing great damage of its own, governments will have to take more control of the firms building it and rewrite economic rules to channel this new power in the right direction.
