articles.title: High School Protests Have French Establishment on the Ropes
articles.author: William Bouchardon
articles.content: It only took a spark to set France ablaze. Protests broke out as the new school year had barely begun, as lycéens (high schoolers, aged roughly fifteen to eighteen) voiced their anger at what they see as neglect and contempt from the government. This deep-rooted discontent recalls earlier episodes. As the movement tries to spread to universities, the authorities’ only answer is repression, and accusations against La France Insoumise (LFI). The radical-left party wants to ride the wave of youth anger in its campaign for next spring’s presidential election, while its opponents hope the movement fizzles out as quickly as possible. France faces zero growth, rising unemployment, soaring fuel prices, the abandonment of ecological policies just as climate change accelerates, and a new austerity budget. Until now, the 2027 presidential election had seemed to be channeling that anger. Ultimately, however, the social explosion is coming from a group that votes little or not at all and feels it has nothing to lose: high schoolers in the Paris region, who were quickly imitated by their peers in the rest of the country. And they have plenty of reasons to be angry. Crumbling Schools and Teacher Shortages It’s no coincidence that the mobilization began in high schools in the poorer towns of the Île-de-France region around Paris, with the first blockades on September 17 in Créteil. Here the new school year was once again marked by extremely degraded teaching conditions. Buildings are often dilapidated: at Paul-Éluard high school in Saint-Denis and Blaise-Cendrars high school in Sevran, videos filmed by students and teachers show, for instance, collapsing ceilings, rats, water leaks, and a shortage of chairs and tables. At Georges-Politzer middle school in Bagnolet (a collège , for ages eleven to fifteen, in another Seine-Saint-Denis town), murky water containing fecal matter came out of every tap, and the school was informed only four months after the tests had been completed. Beyond these particularly shocking examples, school buildings are wholly unsuited to extreme weather events. According to a survey by SNES-FSU , which is the leading teachers’ union in secondary education, covering 623 middle and high schools, this May some 78 percent of schools recorded temperatures above 30 degrees Celsius, and above 33 degrees Celsius in one school out of five. The succession of heat waves that hit France between May and September confirmed this diagnosis, with numerous cases of teachers and students feeling faint, the closure of several hundred schools on the hottest days, and the postponement of baccalauréat exams (the national high school exit exam, which also serves as the university entrance qualification). The académies (the regional branches of the Ministry of National Education) tried to make do and patch things up to deal with the emergency. But at the start of the school year, only 21 percent of schools had planned measures against extreme heat, 61 percent of which consisted of “planned or requested works” — in other words, not yet started. The renovation effort will be gigantic and is already estimated at €40 to €50 billion . The discontent also concerns staff shortages. True, the Ministry of National Education managed to fill almost all the teaching posts offered in this year’s recruitment exam, compared with 91 to 92 percent in 2025, thanks to a reform lowering entry requirements. But some of the new recruits, who hold only a bac+3 (a three-year university degree), must complete two years of training before standing in front of a class; the effect of the reform will therefore not be felt right away. These reassuring figures are also tempered by a drop in the number of posts offered, offset by a greater use of contractuels (contract teachers hired on fixed-term contracts rather than as tenured civil servants), whose training is often very basic. More broadly, the teaching profession is going through a genuine crisis and a “low but steady” rise in resignations, according to the Cour des comptes (France’s public audit body). In the latest Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) survey , only 4 percent of French teachers feel that their profession is valued by society, the lowest level of any country studied. Low pay, below the OECD average, is the leading cause; three-quarters of teachers consider their salary too low. The result is difficulty in delivering all the scheduled classes. At the start of this new school year, half of schools were missing at least one teacher. For the 2023–24 school year, the Cour des comptes estimated that around 9 percent of teaching hours had been lost in middle schools, rising to 11 percent on average in zones d’éducation prioritaire (disadvantaged areas that receive extra resources). This teaching shortfall inevitably weighs on these young people’s level of knowledge and on their professional futures. Despite substantial hiring in recent years, France is also desperately short of AESH (classroom aides for students with disabilities), with nearly 50,000 students, or one in seven, waiting for one at the start of the 2025 school year. The picture is similar for school nurses, with only 7,700 positions for twelve million students in 2023. Despite pay raises for both professions in recent years, salaries remain unattractive. Ever-Deepening Inequalities Beyond these overall figures, the situation varies enormously from one school to another. The académies of Créteil and Versailles, which cover the départements surrounding Paris, have long struggled to attract teachers. Within each académie , the gaps between schools in affluent neighborhoods and those in working-class suburbs ( banlieues populaires ) can also be wide. Early-career teachers are often sent to these disadvantaged areas while they accumulate points to apply for a transfer. Students in these middle and high schools thus face high turnover among less experienced teachers, which worsens their learning conditions. Ministry of National Education data confirm this diagnosis: the “social position index” assigned to each school according to the occupations of its students’ parents reveals major imbalances and strong social reproduction. The correlation between social background and academic achievement among French students is one of the strongest in the OECD. While gaps exist among public schools, they are even wider between public and private education. In 2022, the privately run sector operating under state contract had 40 percent of students from very advantaged backgrounds, against 20 percent in the public sector. Conversely, 18 percent of middle schoolers in these contract private schools came from disadvantaged social classes, against 42 percent of their public sector counterparts. These gaps, which have only widened since the late 1980s, stem from the selectivity practiced by many private schools, based on grades and on the tuition fees charged to parents. Yet these contract private schools are overwhelmingly funded with public money: in 2024, a parliamentary report noted that the state grants €8.5 billion a year to this sector, plus another €1.5 billion from local authorities. The result of a compromise in the long “school war” between the state and the Catholic Church (the great majority of private schools in France are Catholic), the 1959 Debré Law provides that the state covers teachers’ salaries and the running costs of contract schools, amounting to 75 percent of their spending, in exchange for implementing the official curriculum. There are also private schools without a state contract ( hors contrat ), freer in how they operate and receiving no public money, but they educate fewer than 1 percent of French students. On top of these mandatory expenses, some local authorities grant additional subsidies to private schools: between 2016 and 2023, the regions distributed more than €1.2 billion to schools that were already well funded. Although this budgetary lever could allow the state to pressure private schools into promoting greater social diversity, successive ministers have always carefully avoided making such demands. The reason is fairly simple: most of them went through the most prestigious schools (the grandes écoles , France’s highly selective elite institutions) and send their own children to private schools. In 2024, the short-lived National Education Minister Amélie Oudéa-Castéra caused a scandal when she justified placing her children in an extremely upper-class private school — Stanislas high school, in Paris’s 6th arrondissement — by citing teacher absenteeism in the public sector. Her predecessor Gabriel Attal (who went on to become prime minister and is now running for president) himself attended the very bourgeois École alsacienne, in the same neighborhood. These ministers’ school careers are thus emblematic of a form of social separatism. Having grown up in a bourgeois bubble, Macron’s ministers know next to nothing about the social reality of public schools, which often leads them to adopt reforms that hurt the sector even further. At the start of the decade, France had the most overcrowded classes in Europe. For the 2026 school year , a teacher faces an average of twenty-one students in primary school, 25.3 in middle school, and 30.5 in high school. With such numbers, it is hard to support each student properly; inevitably, some are more disruptive and fall behind. The falling birth rate could, however, allow the number of students per teacher to be reduced: by 2035, France will have 1.7 million fewer students , a drop of 14.2 percent. Teachers’ unions, parents, and many politicians see an opportunity: by keeping the number of teachers stable, the ratio can fall naturally over the years. But the government has a different priority: saving money. In 2026, 3,256 teaching positions were cut . The same austerity imperative also led to €40 million being cut from a program of school renovations designed to face climate change, two-thirds of the budget, in the middle of a scorching summer. Phone Bans and Sorting Algorithms Other recent reforms are also fueling the anger, in particular those decided by Gabriel Attal during his time at the Ministry of National Education (July 2023 to January 2024). One is the choc des savoirs (“knowledge shock”), which introduced groupes de niveau (ability-based groups for core subjects), widely denounced by teachers, students, and parents as a form of “social sorting” and whose efficiency has always been disputed . This flagship Attal reform was finally repealed in early 2026. The second measure, adopted in the name of laïcité (France’s strict principle of secularism, which governs the place of religion in public institutions, schools included), is the ban on wearing the abaya (a long, loose-fitting robe worn by some Muslim women), regarded as a religious garment signaling Muslim faith. But this decree, designed to appeal to conservative and far-right voters, proved a headache to enforce: How do you tell an abaya from a dress? Besides the fact that the French Council of the Muslim Faith (a body that represents Muslims in dealings with the state) points out that the abaya has never been a religious garment or prescription, the inconsistent enforcement among girls wearing similar dresses — some having to change, others not — and the fact that only Muslim girls were targeted sparked numerous controversies. Above all, while the goal of secularism is fundamental in national education, one may question if sending young Muslim girls home over a garment rather than letting them attend public school really is the right way to fight Islamic fundamentalism. The ban on mobile phones in high schools since the start of the 2026 school year — already enforced in primary and middle schools — may also have helped stoke the high schoolers’ anger. While the measure clearly has positive effects on students’ focus and public health and helps reduce cheating, the mobile phone remains an often indispensable tool for many school activities. Teachers sometimes ask students to use their phones in class; grades, schedules, and homework are generally conveyed through the Pronote software (the online school-management platform used in most French schools); and the phone also serves as a canteen card. The measure has therefore been applied unevenly , with each school responsible for incorporating it into its internal rules, which inevitably fuels comparisons between students at different schools. Finally, one reform from the early Macron era has never been digested: Parcoursup. This selection algorithm for admission to higher education already sparked fierce anger when it was created in 2018, since it effectively ends the right to access higher education simply by obtaining the baccalauréat. The algorithm’s opacity has not helped. High schoolers send out volleys of applications for the coming university year without being sure what they will end up with. For some, the answer never comes: in July 2026, 100,000 students had no placement for the start of their university studies. Although this figure falls later as places open up, the stress for these young people and their parents is enormous: they end up applying to all kinds of programs, sometimes far from what they want and from where they live, and face great difficulty preparing for the new academic year. Dejected, some wait until the following year to apply again. A History of Student Struggle The combination of these many factors and an especially anxiety-inducing atmosphere — wars, climate change, the rise of the far right, an economy in poor shape — has resulted in extremely poor mental health among young people. For example, 20 percent of high schoolers had suicidal thoughts during the year, according to Santé publique France (the national public health agency). While adolescence has always been a difficult period of human life, such levels are unprecedented and particularly alarming. It therefore did not take much to push high schoolers to launch a social movement, which also gives some of them a reason for hope in the future and a collective fervor they had been deprived of by the reign of screens. Like any youth movement, the current wave of school blockades is chaotic, its demands are sometimes muddled, and its methods do not always command consensus. There are also young people who do not wish to take part in the blockades and are more concerned with passing their exams. The Ministry of National Education is in fact planning video-conference classes for the four hundred to five hundred blockaded high schools in the coming days. A sign of the times, technological tools are now central, both to weaken the movement and to feed it, with Snapchat videos and Instagram posts. But apart from this novelty and the fear of people fainting in suffocating temperatures, the 2026 high school movement has much in common with other historical episodes. Over the past four decades, there has been a major youth movement roughly every ten years, always raising the question of the resources devoted to education. In 2018, a high school and student movement — admittedly smaller than today’s — was launched against Parcoursup and to demand more spots in universities. In 2005, it was the Fillon reform of the baccalauréat, as well as budget cuts, that put high schoolers on the streets. While the government of the day did not back down, it was forced to do so the following year in the face of anger over the CPE (“first employment contract,” which let companies fire young workers without justification during their first two years, adopted with the aim of decreasing youth unemployment). Further back, other mobilizations resemble those of 2026. In October 1998 , high schoolers were already protesting for more teachers and smaller classes and against a general feeling that the future was closed to them. The movement peaked on October 15 with 500,000 protesters across France and won 4 billion francs (roughly €1 billion in today’s value). In 1990 , the movement also began in the Paris suburbs, following the rape of a young girl at a high school in Saint-Ouen. In addition to the fight for safer schools, young people demanded more teachers and the renovation of their run-down schools. The movement led to a package of 4.5 billion francs (roughly €1.2 billion) and to the creation of conseils de la vie lycéenne , which allow elected student representatives to take part in certain decisions at their schools. Will the Blockades Spread to Universities? Can the 2026 wave of school blockades repeat these victories? While it is still too early to say, the answer will depend on its ability to broaden its alliance. After high schools, the next step could be the universities, some of which have already begun to be blockaded . University students indeed share common grievances with high schoolers, such as dilapidated buildings and a lack of space that prevents them from studying in decent conditions. Average spending per student has been falling steadily since 2010, and every French university ran a deficit budget this year. The same logic of inequality and privatization also affects higher education. Faced with a lack of spots in public universities, 26 percent of students chose private higher education in 2022, a share that rises every year. Between 2012 and 2022, the number of students in private higher education rose by 63 percent, against only 3 percent in the public sector. Ranging from excellence to the worst scams, private universities at least have one thing in common: often substantial tuition fees. Student life is getting ever more expensive, and student precarity has risen sharply in recent years, with, for instance, 23 percent of students having already skipped a meal for financial reasons. The 2027 budget is unlikely to improve matters, as it plans to freeze the APL ( aide personnalisée au logement , a means-tested housing benefit that helps pay rent). Always looking for further savings, the government also wanted to introduce fees for students not receiving need-based grants ( non-boursiers ) to attend a BTS ( brevet de technicien supérieur , a two-year vocational higher-education course) or classes préparatoires (the highly selective two-year preparatory courses for the grandes écoles ). The government recently backed down on that idea in the face of high schoolers’ anger. Besides students, high schoolers could also be joined by their teachers, a number of whom already went on strike on September 29 to protest a pay freeze that has lasted for years. Since their demands are often shared, this convergence is fairly obvious. Militant Action and a Hostile Press Besides unions and youth organizations, another player is calling on high schoolers and students to mobilize en masse: La France Insoumise (LFI). The radical-left party led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon very quickly became the political voice of the high schoolers’ demands. Some of its most high-profile figures have been particularly well received by young people at the blockades, such as MP Louis Boyard, himself a former high school student union activist. Many LFI elected officials went to meet the high schoolers from the outset of the movement to encourage them to block their schools, but also to try to defuse tense situations with law enforcement. This presence has drawn heavy criticism on TV talk shows, where LFI has been accused of stirring up chaos and held responsible for damage in several cities. The mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, was thus accused of setting a trash can on fire when he was in fact trying to put it out. As with every social movement, the question of violence quickly dominated media coverage. An analysis of France 2’s evening news broadcasts (France 2 is a major public-service TV channel) over four days shows that 75 percent of the airtime devoted to the high school mobilizations focused on violence and 12 percent on accusations against LFI, while only 8 percent was devoted to the movement’s demands. While most of this violence is limited to burning trash cans and setting off fireworks, some scenes have been striking, such as the burning of a high school entrance in Nantes . As with every social mobilization, the overwhelming majority of participants are of course peaceful, and the unions and political organizations supporting the movement have all called for restraint. But on TV talk shows, LFI is very quickly singled out as responsible for violence and unrest. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu even accused “LFI and its far-left proxies” of being behind the movement, relying on an intelligence service memo that was immediately sent to the media. La France Insoumise has dismissed this thesis as a “ conspiracy ” that “infantilizes” high schoolers and sees it as part of a “strategy of letting things rot and of provocation.” The government’s strategy seems to be partly working: 55 percent of French people surveyed in a recent poll believe the movement is being manipulated by LFI. But another poll indicates that 62 percent of French people consider the high school movement justified. Facing a public that largely backs the young on the one hand, and confronting budgetary restrictions on the other, the government has decided to bet on repression. With the exception of farmers, Emmanuel Macron always applies the same technique to every social movement: crack down on protesters in order to terrorize participants, and exploit the violence to make the movement unpopular. More than five thousand high schoolers were detained in a single week, an unprecedented level. Police violence has also been significant, for example with a grenade fired almost point-blank into the face of a fourteen-year-old in the Val-d’Oise (a département north of Paris). This strategy is risky: in the event of a tragedy — for example the death of a teenager following a police operation — the anger could turn against the police and the government. That is what happened in 1986 with the Malik Oussekine affair, named after a twenty-two-year-old student killed by police during protests against the Devaquet reform, which planned selection for entry to university. Two days after his death, the reform was withdrawn. La France Insoumise and Rassemblement National Confront a Social Movement The high schoolers’ mobilization has in any case surprised the entire political class and brought young people’s malaise back to the forefront of a presidential campaign that had said very little about it until now. With no real answer to offer, the Rassemblement National (RN, the far-right party led by Marine Le Pen ), the traditional right, and the Macronist bloc are betting on the movement running out of steam, hoping to quickly move on to another topic. Marine Le Pen also took the opportunity to criticize the excessive resources supposedly allocated to the banlieues — and therefore to the people with an immigration background who live there — compared with “the forgotten France” of rural areas. The figures, however, disprove this claim, showing average underinvestment of 30 percent per student in Seine-Saint-Denis compared with the rest of the country, even though rural France is also being abandoned by the state. For LFI, the emergence of this social movement is an opportunity to showcase certain points of its program, such as the repeal of Parcoursup and increased resources for national education. If the movement spreads and wins concessions, Jean-Luc Mélenchon will be able to turn it into a campaign argument, claiming that the all-out mobilization strategy he advocates delivers results. The presidential candidate also hopes that this support will persuade young people to vote for him. Particularly popular among the youth, he pays the price for this age group’s low turnout. Conversely, if the movement degenerates and is dominated by violence, LFI risks being held responsible. This social movement, possibly soon joined by a call to revive the gilets jaunes on October 17 to protest rising prices, is in any case a measure of the general atmosphere in France on the eve of a decisive election. Tension is everywhere, and Macronism in its twilight is increasingly overtaken by events and rejected by citizens. Very strong polarization is taking hold between a left-wing camp dominated by La France Insoumise, which intends to build on social struggles, and a radical-right bloc dominated by the Rassemblement National, which is multiplying martial proposals to bring “order” back to the country, without offering any real answers to the social roots of the anger. articles.title: What Comes After Hyperpolitics?
articles.author: Anton Jäger
articles.content: Before the end of this year, the United States will have broken two political records. According to the organizers’ own estimates, No Kings Day on March 28 was the largest single-day protest in recent American history. At the same time, no US president has so successfully enriched himself in office as Donald Trump has — 2026 is set to be the most lucrative year of his career so far. The concept of “hyperpolitics” is an attempt to explain these coincident phenomena. It describes a process of repoliticization without reinstitutionalization that has overtaken every layer of society in the wake of the 2008–9 crash. This surge in political activity has been organizationally uneven, difficult to relate to historical precedents, and, more worryingly, has no guaranteed effect on power relations between elites and masses. In its current iteration, the idea first emerged in this outlet, where it provoked a lively debate. Published in monograph form four years later, Hyperpolitics has also met with varied engagement, both critical and laudatory, from writers across the political spectrum. Even the misreadings have been productive. Part of the reason for returning to these criticisms is that the conversations the book has spawned are not purely of academic interest. Instead, they carry strategic import for the Left, since the book closed on a fundamental question: What can facilitate the rebuilding of class power in the new century, and what locks the Left in the hyperpolitical morass? Generality and Abstraction Hyperpolitics began with an anecdotal observation that then became the basis of a broader theory. The book sought to offer a general description, explanation, and evaluation of a general problem, at an appropriately general level. The danger, of course, is that such generalization can verge on something else: abstractionism, or work that surveys the social terrain at such a distance that it has nothing interesting to say about the meso- or the microlevel. It is this perceived generalism in Hyperpolitics that has bothered a subgroup of readers. Neither a strict work of social science nor pure cultural criticism, the book appears to them as neither fish nor flesh. “If you don’t like my principles, I have others” might be the most convincing Marxian response to this, but I fear the book will have to remain a work of popularization first and foremost. Long-distance lorry drivers do not use the same maps as country hikers. Instead, Hyperpolitics offers a general theory of a general trend — with all the upsides and downsides that generality entails. In the minds of critics, this complaint is often bound up with another issue: a willingness to rely on the insights of writers on the Right as well as on the Left. A simple response to this accusation might be the one the anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss gave, when asked about his reliance on Jean-Jacques Rousseau: “However little I am inclined towards his political thought, the beauty of his prose dazzles me. . . . He says in five words what would take me fifteen.” Yet this response is superficial. There is a deeper reason why the Right proves a more able analyst of bourgeois rot than the Left: reactionaries often have a keener sense of the costs of capitalist progress than liberal leftists do. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels themselves preferred the writings of an archreactionary such as Honoré de Balzac for depictions of the nineteenth century over pious tracts of proletarian literature. As Engels himself put it, “that Balzac was compelled to go against his own class sympathies and political prejudices” and “described the nobles as people deserving no better fate . . . that I consider one of his grandest features.” The Left, dogmatically wedded to liberalism, is often incapable of the kind of curiosity that Marx and Engels saw precisely as an intellectual virtue. Asymmetric Advantage A different critique is that the book offers no explanation of why the far right has seemingly done better out of the new hyperpolitical phase than the Left. Whence this asymmetric advantage? Three facts that the book already touches on but doesn’t expand on bear repeating here — two structural, one more contingent. First, market society gives the Right various basic advantages, as Ralph Miliband observed in his analysis of the “imperfect competition” of liberal democracies. The first of these advantages is ideological. Marx once contrasted the “Party of Progress” to the “Party of Order”: the former tried to modify existing social arrangements, he wrote, while the latter merely wanted to stabilize and consolidate them. Preserving the status quo and securing existing property relations are a much lower benchmark of success. A second, related factor is the availability of private funding. Whether it’s spent on old-style astroturfing or hiring digital influencers, money remains an effective mobilizational tool for the Right but is in scarce supply for the Left (unless we count certain liberal philanthropists who seek to mold a market-friendly socialism). Lacking natural sponsors in the state or in capitalist circles, left-wing projects have also usually had to raise scattered and more financially modest donations. The availability of private money instead gives the Right an unparalleled capacity for mobilization. To this, we can add the power asymmetry in society as a whole, as Perry Anderson has noted: Structurally, by reason of their smaller numbers and greater resources, virtually all ruling classes enjoy an advantage over the ruled in their capacity for collective action. Their internal lines of communication are more compact; their wealth offers an all-purpose medium of power, convertible into any number of forms of domination; their intelligence systems scan the political landscape from a greater height. More numerous and more dispersed, less equipped materially, less armed culturally, subordinate classes always tend, in the sociologist Michael Mann’s phrase, to be “organizationally outflanked.” Yet a third, more contingent factor should also be noted. Within the ranks of the far right, a much bolder debate about the crisis of liberalism has been inaugurated, with some on the Right adopting a consciously “post-liberal” position. Conversely, the current left has a sociological affinity with liberalism — due to the societal groups that comprise it, and due to the Left’s recent academicization — which has slowed an ideological break with it. Otherwise the asymmetry predates the hyperpolitical epoch. Trade-Offs A different facet of the thesis that the book does not theorize concerns correlations between its two analytical axes: the political and the institutional. As critics have noted, these can hardly be said to move independently. Jasper Bernes, for instance, has persuasively argued that across the twentieth century institutionalizing often came at the cost of depoliticizing, while repoliticization often eroded existing institutional structures. In essence, he presents a dilemma between a Weberian ethic of conviction and one of responsibility: to institutionalize might make left-wing politics more durable but also potentially less revolutionary, while a politics with little longevity might be libidinally rewarding but proves unable to unseat existing power structures. These are tricky trade-offs; two case studies may illustrate why. Mao Zedong’s campaign against the party bureaucracy used shock politicization to deinstitutionalize but then ushered in a period of depoliticization later in the century. Inversely, the French and Italian Communist parties’ reaction to the long 1968 in both their countries — a sequence that they saw as an anti-institutional revolt with dangerous political consequences — probably sped up their sclerosis as mass parties in the 1980s. This also made them particularly vulnerable to the neoliberal assault. As Bernes shows, these undulations can thus be mutually coconstituting. In the 1970s, the labor movement was overwhelmed so easily by the neoliberal counterrevolution precisely because it preferred the institutional over the political and was unable to mount a convincing challenge to capital’s retreat from the postwar compact. Hence the general challenge that the book poses: to properly reinstitutionalize the energy released by the hyperpolitical moment. In Bernes’s view, such a reinstitutionalization could be seen from either a communitarian or an interest-based point of view. In the first, the decline of civic life since the 1990s confronts us with a task that is prepolitical rather than political. “What Jäger may be proposing,” he notes, “is a politics of the beer hall without the union shop.” This reading vindicates Bernes’s intuition that “at least in my life, left milieus preserve forms of social life and conviviality fast vanishing elsewhere.” The primary task would then be to rebuild “a sense of belonging, community, and in many cases, satisfaction of real material needs.” In a Tocquevillian vein, this would allow for reinstitutionalization without repoliticization — an antidote to our contemporary loneliness epidemic, for instance, or opportunities for socializing. Yet even bowling clubs require funds, and it is unlikely that members will stay in a union if the union is unable to offer them any wage raises. “If such institutions fail to improve the material fortunes of the vast majority in any durable way,” Bernes wonders, “what success can they claim?” In the age of the long downturn, it is indeed harder to reinstitutionalize by promising members direct benefits. Yet as Vladimir Lenin said, there is no such thing as an impossible situation: the last ten years have demonstrated that a Left without a muscular labor movement is capable of putting itself on the political map but will usually lack the levers to force clear policy change on society. As Sam Gindin put it , the chances for material gains on behalf of labor today might be slimmer, “but what else are you going to be doing with your life?” Reinstitutionalization Hyperpolitics is only a tendency among others, after all, and there are ample signs reinstitutionalization is already underway. The Western left — if the loose collage of organizations and subcultures currently grouped under that rubric can count as a unitary force — finds itself in a contradictory situation in 2026. Many of its causes enjoy growing popular support, but no corresponding institutional strength exists to translate these causes into direct concessions from capital. Since 2008, the policy consensus of the neoliberal era has clearly fractured, but this has done little to increase the power of labor or the Left as such; most of the social movements that emerged in the 2010s have proven incapable of reversing these trends. Such an uneven revival has encouraged two competing yet not necessarily irreconcilable left-wing tendencies. The first is what we might term “immediatism.” This insists on the notion that the new energies spawned by online platforms can provide the basis for a return of mass politics, organized around a response to various online “viral” phenomena that can repoliticize an atomized mass glued to their screens and direct them for an insurrectionary assault on the capitalist state. This is a proposition much in favor with some post-Trotskyite grouplets but also left communists and anarchists, whose politics never presupposed a solidly organized labor movement. Many of these proposals are hardly new and are reminiscent of Alexander Herzen’s critique of the Russian radical Mikhail Bakunin, who allegedly had a tendency “to mistake the second month of a pregnancy for the ninth.” A second tendency at least recognizes the need for reinstitutionalization but seeks to personalize it: the left-populism proposed by Chantal Mouffe and Ernesto Laclau, above all, who sought to offer a left-wing variant of leaderism. The influence of these ideas is visible in the “gaseous party” built by Jean-Luc Mélenchon or the shenanigans surrounding Jeremy Corbyn’s Your Party. Unifying both approaches is a wish to magically conjure up a form of politics that took the Left decades to build in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, without the corresponding class power. What would a slower reinstitutionalization look like in practice? Against the impatience of hyperpolitics, many have advised a return to Karl Kautsky’s original pre–World War I “strategy of patience.” In Kautsky’s vision, institutionalization and politicization move on two overlapping timelines: one long-, the other short-term. For the first, clear institutional agents — cooperatives, unions, parties — can be activated in times of sharpening class tension but otherwise need to bide their time in the trenches. Such an approach would balance spontaneity and organization. It also seems helpful in our time of mounting politicization without accompanying institutional heft. A defense of this neo-Kautskyite approach must be strictly conditional, of course. The man himself ended up as an anti-Bolshevik scab, demonstrating that pleas against impatience can easily slide into reformist accommodation. Institutionalization, we see here, is by no means intrinsically revolutionary. As Bernes indicated, it might even be the reason why a revolutionary breakthrough was not achieved in Kautsky’s own country and age: the labor movement’s upper cadres sought to temper the base because they thought institution-building in capitalism was more important than political breaks with it. Fossilization was the most likely consequence. Genetic Manipulation Few of those institutional dinosaurs survive today, as Bernes notes too. There are some mass parties that have weathered the postpolitical ice age and the hyperpolitical thaw — one could think of the Communist Party in Greece — yet they mostly retain interest as historical curiosities. Everyone agrees that you cannot clone a dinosaur. Yet as scientists know, genetic manipulation is not impossible either, even if one needs a sense of the material one is working with. As Dylan Riley has noted, the task of the contemporary left is the “creation of a new modern prince adapted to the age of social media, virality and artificial intelligence, in addition to the ubiquitous culture industry,” which would not immediately succumb to the new liquidity. Here the recent trajectory of the Workers’ Party of Belgium (PTB/PVDA) at least warrants a mention. The PTB is modeled on a Maoist cadre party. It has a predictable “Marxist-Leninist” ban on factions, a multitiered membership model, and record numbers on Belgian social media. Uniquely among Belgian and European parties, however, the PTB has had measurable success in growing its base in recent years. It has established closer ties with Belgium’s still multitudinous union movement. It sees its parliamentary role as that of a popular tribune rather than a candidate for rule. It has also obstructed several governments’ attempts to complete the neoliberal restructuring of Belgian society, long finished in neighboring countries. For all its pathologies, the party proves that patience pays. (It is historically revealing, of course, that the PTB would be horrified at the idea of being labeled “Kautskyite,” which bears testimony to the century of changes that lies behind us.) The Kautskyism of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is a wholly different creature. Officially, DSA is not even a party but a “socialist organization,” as members do not cease to point out. As Joe Todd has noted in a comparative study of both, the PTB and DSA evince some radical differences too, even if they are often cited together. Unlike the PTB’s more centralized power structure, DSA is informally distributed between chapters and caucuses. Such an absence of strict centralism also means that the organization has greater difficulty drawing a line between internal debate and external messaging. Unlike the PTB, its membership model is flat rather than tiered, allowing for easier entry. Its leadership is relatively flexible in comparison too, while its caucuses enjoy a much greater degree of autonomy than local PTB branches do. Most likely, the historical anti-Stalinism of DSA is responsible for this relative lack of centralism. Both the PTB and DSA have experienced significant growth in the past decade, in terms of members and wider societal influence. Yet the key question, as usual, is Lenin’s: Who leads whom? This is particularly important for the prospect of an Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez presidential run. Will DSA end up as a campaign vehicle for left-leaning members of Congress eyeing careers in the DNC, or will it be a disciplining force for lawmakers who use the Democrats as a mere platform but maintain their political independence? The jury is still out on the question, but it is worth spelling out the risks of both models. Like any work of social science, Hyperpolitics is neither a self-help handbook nor a horoscope for our political future. All that can be done is to point out tendencies and probabilities; there is no iron law decreeing either the persistence or the instant evanescence of hyperpolitics today. Reinstitutionalization is hard, particularly in today’s economic environment in which growth is concentrated at the top of society, and the competitors for the Left’s pro-social program are well-funded and at ease with power. Yet the race for reinstitutionalization has opened; what Hyperpolitics sought to do, above all, was to make clear the difference between escape routes and dead ends. articles.title: Andy Burnham’s Labour Allows the Left to Breathe, a Little
articles.author: Harry Williams
articles.content: “For too long, politics has not been working for people across Britain. We need to do better, and we will.” Such was Andy Burnham’s welcome to this year’s Labour Party conference. Gemma Bolton, a left-wing member of the party’s National Executive Committee, more simply summed up the change after years of purges, suspensions and rigged candidate selections: “Isn’t it nice you can breathe again?” This is roughly Burnham’s fortieth Labour conference, but his first as prime minister. His acclamation as party leader in July and this conference have been a break with the recent past under both Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer, but in many ways represent a return to a much more traditional form of Labour politics. It’s a line often called the “soft left” or a “Blue Labour” appeal to the traditional working class but is best understood by the party’s own name: Labourism. Conference Tradition On one level, Labour’s annual conference is like any other in British politics. Party leaders use them to announce policy and direction for their time in opposition or in government. This provides the bulk of media analysis. But while this is important, Labour’s internal life, and by extension how it governs, can’t be understood without grasping the history of its annual meeting. For Labour conferences are in another sense quite unique. Unlike Reform UK or the Tories’ public relations rallies, or the messy free-for-alls of Liberal Democrat or Green internal democracy, the Labour conference is essentially modeled on trade union practice. Being born of the labor movement (the party is the result of an 1899 Trades Union Congress resolution), this is no great surprise. It is, however, something of an anachronism in a country where union membership has been in the doldrums for decades. The conference acts in theory as a sovereign meeting of the organizations that make up the Labour Party and is meant to direct the actions of its parliamentary leadership. Delegates mainly represent either local level parties or trade unions. While most uncontentious votes are settled by a show of hands, a close decision goes to a “card vote.” Then each delegate’s vote is weighted according to organizational size. Hence the Wigan Pier Constituency Labour Party, with three delegates (representing two hundred members) could be outvoted by one delegate for the Wheel Tappers and Shunters Association (representing two thousand members). There is no official voting delegation for the Parliamentary Labour Party (PLP), but the formal subordination of MPs to the wider party belies the historical reality. Since the party’s inception, the PLP has often asserted its independence from conference decisions. As in most social democratic parties, this has often resulted in left-wing policy piling up at the conference but right-wing decisions being taken by MPs. This tension came to a head in the 1970s, when the 1974 election manifesto (soon becoming the basis of Bennism ) was largely junked by the PLP once in office. The resulting outrage among members saw the creation of the left-wing Campaign for Labour Party Democracy ( CLPD ). Its focus was on “power: where power is found within the party and how to achieve greater democratic control of it.” In this same period, the aforementioned “soft left” — defined by support for left-wing policy goals while also believing in deference to the (more right-wing) PLP’s independence — started to coalesce around the Tribune Group of MPs. A high point in victories for the Left and party democracy in the 1980s culminated in Tony Benn’s only narrow defeat to Denis Healey in the 1981 deputy leadership election. As the 1980s and ’90s progressed, a succession of right-wing leaderships saw the conference’s nominal sovereignty eroded and increasingly ignored. In the Blairite era, conferences came to resemble their Tory counterparts: that is, PR exercises for party elites and allied trades such as lobbyists and consultants. The conference itself slowly migrated from cheap seaside towns, ideal for trade unionists and constituency delegates, to big cities providing better options for New Labour charm offensives, as captured by Jarvis Cocker. Corbynism saw a brief restoration of the conference’s vitality, with the World Transformed festival and heated contests over Brexit and the selection of MPs. Arriving as leader in 2020, Starmer’s overwhelming priority was to smash this flowering of democratic participation, and he was largely successful . Long before Starmer’s polling collapse and ignominious fall this summer, the conference had returned to a mere husk of democratic organization orchestrated by the leadership. Enter Burnham How does Burnham’s first conference contrast with this history? In terms of conference official business, the CLPD/Momentum efforts to promote democratization did little better than they had over the last few years. The same was true of policy motions concerning Cuba and Palestine abroad or public ownership and National Health Service funding at home. Motions were either voted down or not heard, ruled out on spurious grounds. Committees elected by the conference produced near clean sweeps for the party’s antidemocratic neoliberal right wing. Despite this, the organized left-wing presence on the conference floor was larger than in recent years under Starmer. In part this was due to improved organization by the traditional CLPD/Momentum organized left. It was also due to a reorientation by the soft left from the right-leaning Fabian/Brownite Open Labour to a left-leaning group called Mainstream. Mainstream was launched at the 2025 conference by the soft-left figure and Compass director, Neal Lawson, backed by Burnham (at the time mayor of Manchester), seemingly unhappy with the existing soft-left membership organization, Open Labour. Mainstream’s position could be boiled down to a feeling that Starmer’s counterrevolution had gone too far. Starmer had run for the leadership in 2020, outwardly proposing a progressive but competent “Corbynism without Corbyn” before striking hard to the right. This same slogan might well define Mainstream’s 2026 position of “Manchesterism,” modeled on Burnham’s record as mayor. As a policy platform, this tries to balance a “market middle” and “innovation frontier” economy with a much more radical “decommodified provision of essentials. . . . organised around affordability, universal access, environmental sustainability, and worker welfare. This tier provides security: no one can fall below it because access is unconditional.” Despite capturing the current zeitgeist of the party and arguably Britain itself, Mainstream has limitations — on its own terms and for the socialist left. As a faction defined by opposing “factionalism,” soft-left support for progressive policy (the “Corbynism” bit) combined with its reluctance to challenge the state/party machine head-on (the “without Corbyn” bit) leaves a political and organizational muddle. For all the media buzz and high profile figures at its events, the soft left struggles to coherently define itself against Labour’s traditional right or left. The result is an organization with a very broad but shallow support, which struggles to take on still-dominant Blairite factions in party elections or even to settle on clear structures. In the first two key electoral tests it has faced (Labour’s NEC and conference delegate elections) it has done little better than Labour’s much smaller and more polarizing (though politically clearer and better-organized) factions. If Mainstream remains unable to overcome this muddle, it may well fall out of the limelight much like now-dissolved Open Labour before it. While initially welcoming Mainstream’s creation, Burnham has been lukewarm about it since he became party leader. However, the key difference in conference business compared to recent years reflects the political change Burnham represents. The parliamentary leadership has regained the confidence of the affiliated trade unions. Historically, unions and their powerful bloc vote have acted as the support base needed by Labour leaders to block left-wing rule changes or policies emanating from members. However, as the Labour right steadily dropped its social democratic commitments just as unions needed them most, this relationship came under increasing strain. The peak of this rift saw several unions backing veteran CLPD member Corbyn for Labour leader in the 2010s (a relationship with its own discomforts). Most unions reverted to type in Starmer’s early years as leader, but after he took office as prime minister in 2024, the relationship again began to break down amid deeply unpopular austerity measures such as the winter fuel cuts and his approach to the Gaza genocide . This year, with the exception of an overwhelming union boycott of Women’s Conference over transphobia, saw no such public disagreements. This rapprochement signifies how Burnham is trying to return to a much older form of postwar Labour politics. The collapse of the British labor movement industrially saw its political project slacken and drift away from it. “Old Labour” became the main bogeyman of Tony Blair’s New Labour. Its modernizing image had no room for blue-collar workers. An increasingly disorganized and post-political working class made no lasting attempt to fight this drift. Corbynism, while a reaction against the neoliberal project, equally struggled to turn its close alignment with unions’ economic demands into a lasting penetration of the so-called red wall of lost Labour heartlands. The Starmerite attempt to rebuild Labour inside this literal and metaphorical constituency was labeled in the press as a “Blue Labour” strategy. This fundamental misreading of the social sector in question reduced Labour-inclined small town factory workers and lorry drivers (workers with largely progressive values alongside more residual social conservatism than urban Labour voters) to the caricature of the reactionary, essentially Thatcherite “white van man.” The result was endless attempts to ape Nigel Farage’s Reform UK on everything from immigration and welfare to Palestine and drugs in the hope of “winning back” a right-wing party’s core vote. Nowhere was this misstep clearer than Starmerism’s relentless and bizarre focus on winning votes back from the Greens by highlighting how left wing this rival party was. Burnhamism has seen an immediate break with this second-time-as-farce Blairism. The pledges announced at the conference by Burnham and other ministers place the party firmly within the common sense of center-left Britain. Most were relatively mild, such as commitments to more apprenticeships and the Union Learning Fund. Some had less policy impact but profound symbolic significance, like Ed Miliband’s “apology” to the public over Gaza. Burnham and Miliband also avoided the Labour Friends of Israel ’s reception, while Deputy Leader Lucy Powell noticed glum faces at the right-wing-controlled Jewish Labour Movement reception. Some commitments, such as creating a National Social Care Service, renegotiating ties with Europe, and reforms to the voting system, could be huge transformations to how the country lives and is governed. Other pledges were clear responses to trade union pressure. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander’s announcement on “RoSCos” (publicly owned train companies) answered a long-standing campaign by the rail unions. Likewise, Louise Haigh’s commitment to a national insourcing unit took place in the hall while a joint RMT-Unison Insource Now! rally took place outside. The details on many of these policies are vague or contradictory, largely more modest than the “Manchesterism” promised in the Mainstream/Commonwealth pamphlet, and the style is much more timid than the combative tone Burnham adopted toward vested interests like bond markets before his return to parliament this summer. The Home Office in particular remains a source of straightforwardly reactionary initiatives . It falls well short of the programs Labour fought the 2017 and 2019 elections on. Both in tone and in content, Corbynism this is not. Burnhamism instead represents a last roll of the dice for a small-c conservative working-class politics that tries to turn the labor movement’s common sense into a national program for government. In this sense, it has far more in common with the Labour governments of 1945 and 1964 (in spirit if not in scale) than it does with any Labour project since the millennium. It looks like a return of Labourism after thirty years of Labour leaderships that have tried much sharper though perhaps more brittle projects. But will this work? And what does this mean for the Left? So far, Burnham’s strong approval ratings suggest it is working, at least electorally. How long this will hold depends on whether it works socially when the state implements this program. Passing resemblances to Bidenism should be treated as a warning sign. For the Left, it must be clear that this highly uneven leftward shift doesn’t deserve uncritical cheerleading. Already, MPs from the Socialist Campaign Group (SCG) have written articles pushing back against elements of the party platform announced at the conference. The Left outside of the party in social and labor movements will also likely find itself in direct conflict with the government. It is not the job of the Labour left to try and discipline these comrades at the behest of the parliamentary leadership. The SCG launching its own program at the conference was a welcome step forward. The wider left also needs to regain some perspective. Already a joke by the SCG chair about wrapping up the organization for Burnham has led to online denunciations of betrayal. The last ten years in Labour politics have made it easy to deal in absolutes. Corbynism represented the greatest opportunity for socialism in Britain for a century. Starmerism was capital using the primary political institution of the labor movement to wage an unrelenting war on socialists. The Labour right still retains a vanguardist adherence to a failed 2000s political project. The PLP Starmerites would have continued their headlong rush to electoral Armageddon if not stopped. Had the Left and soft left not stayed and wrestled the party back from the right, there would be no Prime Minister Burnham or Manchesterism to face down Reform UK in 2029. Even now Starmerite loyalists are getting ready to steer the new government rightward or derail it in the attempt. This is a big risk. Burnham has an insecure mandate and his “ism” is an opportunistic/pragmatic ideology. It will take a committed socialist left in Labour to make sure Burnham delivers the progressive vision he set out last week. articles.content: We recruited the 400th member of Pinellas DSA this month — and we’re still growing! BOO, comrade! An extra-spooky Halloween edition of the Pinellas DSA newsletter is here! We hit another exciting milestone in September — our chapter is now officially more than 400 members strong! That’s 400 friends and neighbors who’ve made the choice to stand up and say “I believe that a better world is possible.” And, as long as we keep doing the day-to-day work of building our organization and growing the international movement for socialism, we will transform possible into inevitable . Read on to learn more about what our chapter was up to over the last month, and what we have coming up next! September Highlights PDSA comrades at the September Interest Meeting & New Member Orientation. September was a month of steady progress for our ongoing campaigns. Perhaps the biggest development came early in the month when DSA comrades behind the Dump Duke campaign held a press conference in Williams Park to announce the launch of a petition campaign to place an amendment for public power on the 2028 ballot. Meanwhile, organizers behind the No on 3 initiative wasted no time, launching a series of door-to-door canvasses, lit drops, and more to get the word out about the threat Amendment 3 poses to our communities. We also established a social media presence for our DeFlock St. Pete campaign, which has already seen a major win with a new business item in front of the St. Pete City Council, introduced by Councilmember and DSA comrade Richie Floyd, to allow for the discussion of the city’s Flock contract. We also published the first in a fantastic new series of videos from our International Solidarity Working Group, with the aim of educating the masses on the legacy of US imperialism in the Caribbean. Check it out on the official Pinellas DSA YouTube channel (and subscribe while you’re at it)! Lastly, we want to also spotlight the Pinellas DSA blog , which is where you can find updates and official statements published on behalf of the chapter. We’re also accepting submissions for the blog from any active member in good standing; email us at dsa.pinellas@gmail.com if you’d like to pitch your article! CAMPAIGN UPDATE: Dump Duke On September 2, Pinellas DSA members held a press conference to announce the launch of a petition campaign to place a charter amendment on the 2028 ballot. If successful, the initiative would give St. Pete voters the opportunity to decide whether the city should establish a publicly owned electric utility. The event, which was held in Williams Park — directly across the street from Duke Energy headquarters — was also the official launch of Public Power St. Pete, a coalition aimed at advancing the #DumpDuke mission. Besides Pinellas DSA, other coalition members include the CLEO Institute, Sierra Club Suncoast Group, Florida Youth Action Fund, People Power for Florida, and Florida Rising. At the heart of this campaign is a simple goal: making electricity more affordable, reliable, and locally controlled for St. Pete residents. It won’t be easy, though: organizers will need to collect 16,200 petitions with verified signatures from St. Pete voters, with the aim to secure over 20,000 signatures. Learn more about the petition drive here CAMPAIGN UPDATE: DeFlock St. Pete As mentioned above, Councilmember Richie Floyd introducing a business item during a meeting of the St. Pete City Council at the end of August to allow for the discussion of the city’s Flock contract. Specifically, how we can eliminate it . You might reasonably assume that this initiative would see pushback from at least a few of the council’s more conservative members. However, St. Pete City Council voted unanimously to pass this item, and advance the discussion to the city’s Public Services & Infrastructure Committee. Richie sits on the committee, as do Councilmembers Hanewicz, Harting, and Gerdes. Organizers with the DeFlock St. Pete campaign are asking anyone who is “passionate about preventing our little slice of Florida from becoming part of the surveillance state” to reach out to the three committee members in question, thank them for backing Richie’s business item, and let them know that you want to #DeFlockStPete! You can reach the officials in question using the contact information provided below: Copley Gerdes: copley.gerdes@stpete.org | (727) 551–3528 Mike Harting: mike.harting@stpete.org | (727) 551–3305 Lisset Hanewicz: lisset.hanewicz@stpete.org | (727) 893–7412 CAMPAIGN UPDATE: No on 3 PDSA comrades out knocking doors to get out the vote against Amendment 3. Organizers behind the No on 3 campaign hit the ground running last month, launching into a series of door-to-door canvasses, lit drops, and “public service stakeouts” to rally Pinellas residents to defeat Amendment 3 on the November ballot. If Amendment 3 passes, Pinellas County residents will suffer from millions of dollars in public funding cuts each year, impacting EMS, fire and rescue, flood mitigation, infrastructure repair, libraries, parks, public transit, and more. This campaign was spun up on short notice, withe less than three months to get the word out. But, organizers have done a phenomenal job so far! articles.title: Interest Rate Increases Are About Disciplining Labor
articles.author: Arthur MacEwan
articles.content: Using its favored policy in the face of inflation, the Federal Reserve Board, under its new chairman, Kevin Warsh, pushed up short-term interest rates in September. This action may have some impact on the rate of inflation, but probably not much. Raising interest rates may curtail inflation under some circumstances, but the major factors bringing about the current, continuing inflation are unlikely to be much affected by the Fed’s recent interest rate increases. But those other factors are out of bounds: the Fed can’t alter them, and the current administration in Washington won’t. What Washington Has Done to Curtail Inflation With the emergence of economic instability in the early 1970s, President Richard Nixon imposed wage-price controls that limited how much wages and prices could rise. To oversee wage-price controls, his administration established two agencies, a Pay Board and a Cost of Living Council. Economist Arnold Weber was the executive director of the Cost of Living Council and a member of the Pay Board. In 1974, Weber summed up the actions that these federal institutions had undertaken to contain inflation with this statement , “The goal here is to zap labor. That’s what we’re doing here. . . . We have to zap labor.” Attempting to quell inflation in 2022 by pushing interest rates up, then–Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board Jerome Powell saw the problem this way : “ . . . look at the average hourly earnings number we got with the last payrolls report. You don’t really see much progress in terms of average hourly earnings coming down.” Whether the mechanism was wage-price controls, raising interest rates, zapping labor, or, as Powell proclaimed, viewing “progress in terms of average hourly earnings coming down,” the authorities in Washington have been consistent in the way they have seen policy bringing about a reduction of inflation. Since the 1970s, the favored mechanism has been for the Fed to raise interest rates. The rationale is simple: raising interest rates makes it more costly to borrow money, and this leads both businesses and households to hold off on spending (fewer new factories, reduced housing construction, and fewer car purchases, for example). This reduction in investment lessens hiring and costs some workers their jobs. That in turn weakens the bargaining power of workers, leading to lower wages, or at least slower wage increases. As the wage bill of employers (how much employers spend on labor) grows more slowly and the buying power of workers ebbs, prices will tend to fall, or at least not rise so rapidly. This policy has its greatest impact on workers, many of whom lose their jobs, and almost all are in a weaker position to attain wage gains. Yes, businesses can be hurt too in these circumstances. Yet for those who make the policies, the primary problem is that wages are getting out of hand, and it is workers who will bear the burden of the policy. Moreover, the impact on labor tends to have the long-run effect of weakening the power of workers. The most dramatic application of this anti-inflation policy took place in the early 1980s. Prices, as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), rose at an annual rate of more than 10 percent between mid-1977 and mid-1981. By the middle of 1981, the Fed had pushed up the Federal Funds Effective Rate (FFER) to over 20 percent, and that rate did not fall below 10 percent until August 1982. (The FFER is the interest rate banks charge on overnight loans to each other, and it is the rate most immediately affected by Fed actions.) It worked. Inflation abated, running at an annual rate of less than 3 percent in the mid-1980s. And unemployment? The unemployment rate rose to 10.8 percent at the end of 1982, the highest monthly rate since World War II, except for some months during the pandemic of the early 2020s. And wages? The average wages for all workers fell off between the 1970s and 1980, and, for workers in the bottom half (by wage level) of the labor force, it wasn’t until the mid-1990s that wages again reached the level of the 1970s. Labor had been zapped. So why won’t it work this time? Causes of the Current Inflation Higher interest rates tend to stop or slow inflation by reducing aggregate demand — that is, overall spending in the economy — thus curtailing employment, pushing wages down, and thereby reducing inflation. However, it is hard to blame wages for the current inflation when labor costs have not been rising as fast as prices. The Financial Times reports that the rate of labor costs per unit of output — that is, the labor cost of producing a given amount of goods and services — “over the last four years has averaged 2 percent and during the past year is running at 1.5 percent,” both of which are less than the rate of inflation. And, according to The Financial Times , “over the last 12 months, average hourly earnings have risen at the slowest pace in seven years.” Furthermore, the share of national output going to labor — that is, the portion of the economy’s income paid to workers — is lower than at any time since World War II, having fallen from between 61 percent and 66 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the 1960s to 53 percent of GDP today. In any case, important causes of the current inflation are not demand problems. Some are instead supply problems — shortages or higher costs that limit the amount of goods and services available — that have followed from the perverse policies of the Trump administration: The war that the United States initiated against Iran has had severe impacts on the price of oil and oil-based products (especially fertilizer). The high price of oil feeds through the whole economy, as is starkly seen in the way the price of diesel fuel, which was $6.51 per gallon in late September, has affected the cost of transporting goods. The Trump administration’s imposition of tariffs has had an across-the-board impact on prices. Not only are the prices of the imported goods themselves raised, but much of what the United States imports is used as an input for domestically produced goods — automobiles are a well-known and important example. A less well-known example was pointed out in 2021 by The Economist : “Pfizer’s [covid] vaccine requires 280 inputs from suppliers in 19 countries. No firm can recreate that in a hurry.” Because complex international supply chains cannot be changed quickly, tariffs tend to push up the costs of many goods that are not directly affected by the tariffs. The massive campaign by the Trump administration to push immigrants out of the country has led to significant labor shortages in several industries — construction, meatpacking, and agriculture are all examples. According to the White House , “The Trump administration has deported more than 605,000 illegal aliens, with an additional 1.9 million self-deporting, bringing the total number of illegals who have left the U.S. since President Trump returned to office to over 2.5 million.” Labor supply shortages tend to push up prices. Not all of the factors bringing about the recent inflation are on the supply side. Yet two important demand factors are unlikely to be substantially affected by the Fed’s effort to push up interest rates. One of these factors is the large government deficit, a consequence of large tax reductions for the wealthy without a matching decrease of spending — as cuts to programs for the poor have been offset by increases in military spending. (Not only has the Republican congress legislated tax reductions, especially for the wealthy, but there is also the failure of the IRS to halt tax evasion.) It is possible, of course, that higher interest rates, which are also increasing the costs of government debt payments, might bring some sanity to the federal budget, but this seems unlikely. Moreover, interest rates on Treasury bonds, the cost of government debt payments, are already higher than at any time in the last two decades. The other demand factor contributing to inflation is the enormous investment in data centers being constructed to support artificial intelligence. These data centers are leading to electricity price increases in several parts of the country, and the expenditure on their construction is keeping aggregate demand strong. Of course, much of the expenditures on data centers is financed by debt, and the taking on of debt might be reduced by rising interest rates. But it seems that companies such as Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet (Google) are unlikely to substantially slow their activity because of interest rate hikes. For them, artificial intelligence promises the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. The Trump administration is very unlikely to cease its military actions in the Middle East (and elsewhere), to abandon the tariffs, or to stop pushing people out of the country — all of which affect prices by disruption of supply. And the government deficit and the massive expenditures on data centers are unlikely to be seriously affected by the Fed’s action on interest rates. So, when all else is out of bounds, zap labor. An Afterword I cannot help but comment on the irony that, while progressive economists have long been critical of, and generally opposed to, the Fed using rate hikes to quell inflation, today it is President Donald Trump who is doing so with his rants for lower interest rates. I can defend those of us on the Left by pointing out that we have opposed the supply-related policies noted above — the military actions, the inane tariffs, and the expulsion of people who have come here to work (and who pay taxes). Also, we have opposed the tax cuts for the wealthy and military spending that have fueled the inflation, and we are not at all happy with the push to build data centers. Dealing with these issues could reduce inflation without zapping labor (though electricians working on the data centers might object). Trump, however, seems oblivious to even the existence of an inflation problem and its severe effects on the cost of living. He seems to think that the important issue is keeping interest rates low as a means of pushing economic growth and keeping the stock market booming. It appears, however, that inflation has more people (voters) agitated than slow economic growth or a possible stock market slump. But while I may be able to explain why progressive economists think the way we do, I make no attempt to explain the president’s thinking! articles.title: Why Organize Semiconductor Workers? w/ CHIPS Communities United
articles.content: Block & Build is a weekly newsmagazine podcast from Convergence Magazine that examines the balance of political forces in the US from a movement perspective. Every week, host Cayden Mak explores what's… This is the last article. Subscribe to our email newsletter to get more. Semiconductors are at the heart of every piece of electronics you interact with on a daily basis. Despite being invented and innovated in the US, much of the manufacturing of semiconductors and the technology they power was “offshored” from the 1980s through the early 2000s as part of the globalization of our economy. In an effort to counter that loss of jobs and industry, the Biden administration passed the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, which reinvests over $50 billion domestically in the manufacturing and research of semiconductors in the United States. While this has started to proffer new work opportunities and industrial development in the US, workers in the industry are organizing for wall-to-wall unions in their facilities as well as better conditions for the communities that house them. The result of that organizing is CHIPS Communities United , a coalition organizing for an equitable and sustainable semiconductor manufacturing industry. Their alliance includes labor, environmental, social justice, civil rights, and community organizations representing millions of workers and community members nationwide. Their vision is to win well-paying union jobs for all workers in semiconductor factories, to protect local environments, and to keep workers, their families, and community members safe from toxic chemicals. This week’s guests include Rand Wilson, a CCU Organizer with more than 40 years of experience working with a number of national and local unions; Joe Turmes, a Boise, Idaho, based engineer, artist, and activist who has spent nearly 30 years in the semiconductor industry, currently at Micron; and Max (appearing pseudonymously to protect their identity), a fab tech based in Oregon currently working to unionize their workplace.
